India His form is beautiful with the luster of the moon at the end of the Kalpa; he is delightful with the resonant sound of his tinkling speech (or *vaṇu*).
May the Beloved of the Gopīs—who, dwelling in the heart, agitates the three worlds—be for your prosperity.

Having discerned here that which was spoken by Nārada and others, I shall describe the ritual of worship for the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, receiving upon my head the most excellent particles of dust from the two lotus-feet of my guru.
For among those born of the four classes— the Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras— and among those of the various orders— the forest-dwelling sages, hermits, and householders—
certain mantras indeed bear fruit for certain individuals in certain ways through recitation, oblation, sacrifice, and other rites.
Among all castes, as well as among those in the various stages of life, and among women of diverse names and births—
this Gopālaka mantra is the swift bestower of all desired fruits.
Devotion quickly becomes the instrument for attaining the falling of the glances of the Infallible One;
therefore, for the sake of obtaining those four fruits, one who possesses devotion is qualified toward both Hari and the Guru.

Having bathed, wearing clean, fine, and pure garments, with hands, feet, and face washed, being self-composed, his hands marked with the sacred *pavitra*, radiant with white vertical *puṇḍra* marks, facing the east and having firmly assumed the *padmāsana* or *svastika* posture, he should sit comfortably and then salute his own guru and Gaṇeśa.
Having joined his palms in reverence.
Then, having purified his two hands with the Astra-mantra, and having performed the triple-clap (tritāla), the binding of the directions (digbandha), and the fire-chamber (hūtāśaśālā),
the one of pure intellect should gradually purify this body, which consists of the elements (bhūta).
The practitioner of mantra should first visualize the seed-syllable of Satatagati (the Wind), accompanied by the *lavaka* (the nasal bindu), as smoke-colored;

it causes the drying up of all worlds. Having filled his entire body with that [wind] like the pervasive sun and having completely dried it up, he should then release the breath through the path of the Sun (the right nostril).
Having meditated upon the seed-syllable of the fire-god as red and its wind having dissolved through that very path,
one should fill the body and, after thoroughly burning it, release the breath from the left side along with the ashes outside.
May [the practitioner] lead the Moon, which is exceedingly pure and consists of nectar, from the moon on his forehead along the path of the *amṛta* syllables;
then, having caused it to descend by means of the recitation of the *la*-syllable, he should fashion with that [nectar] his entire body as a shower of floods of nectar.
This [is characterized by] faces, hands, and so forth.
One should place [the letters] in sequence upon the head, face, conduct, eyes, ears, nose, cheeks, both lips, the two rows of teeth, and the head and mouth;
and the *hal* consonants with care upon the joints of the hands and feet, their tips, the pair of sides, the back, and the navel.
The wise one should place the *ṣā* syllables upon the children;
having placed them on the heart, the armpits, the back, the roots of the hands, the pair of feet, the belly, and the mouth,
he should then, starting from the heart, place the *andhaṃ* syllables along this same path.
For the sake of accomplishing a pure body,
having thus performed the preliminary practice with those fifty syllables of the body, which are beautified by the half-moon and the visarga;

Having performed the placement [of the syllables], one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) in sequence with the forms beginning with Keśava, accompanied by the Śaktis such as Kīrti and the rest.
Now I shall describe the forms and Śaktis of the phonemes, which consist of the entire universe:
Keśava and Kīrti, Nārāyaṇa and Kānti, and likewise Mādhava and Tuṣṭi.
Govinda is endowed with nourishment, Viṣṇu with fortitude, Sūdana is the beginning of the Madhus, and Śānti is the primordial one;
Trivikrama is action, and Vāmana is endowed with compassion.
Medhā is joined with Śrīdhara, and Hṛṣīkanātha is joined with Harṣā;
Ambujanābha is joined with Śraddhā, and Dāmodara is again joined with Lajjā.
Lakṣmī with Vāsudeva; Saṅkarṣaṇa joined with Sarasvatī; Pradyumna accompanied by Śrī; Aniruddha together with Rati—these [deities] are endowed with their respective consorts.

Cakrijayā, Gadidurgā, and Śārṅginī are likewise endowed with splendor; Satyā is the bearer of the conch, Caṇḍā is the wielder of the plow, Bāṇī is the holder of the arrow, and Mūṣalinī is the consort of the wielder of the club.
Śūlin, Vijayā, Pāśin, Virajā, Viśvānvita, Aṅkuśin;
furthermore, Vinadā joined with Mukunda, Smṛti joined with Nandaja, and [Smṛti] joined with Nandin.
Nara is endowed with *ṛddhi*, Naraka-jit is endowed with *samṛddhi*, and then Śuddhi-yug-dhara;
Kṛṣṇa is joined with *buddhi*, Satya is joined with *śakti*, and Sātvata Śauri is joined with *mati*.
Śūra is endowed with *kṣamā*, Janārdana with *ramā*, and Mā-bhūdhara is endowed with *kleda*.
Klinnā is endowed with the Viśvādi-forms, and likewise Vasudhā is joined with Vaikuṇṭha;
Puruṣottama is Vasudā, and [she] is accompanied by Valinā and Parā; [she] is further joined with Balānuja and is known as Parāyaṇā; then there are Vāla, Sūkṣmā, and Vṛṣaghnasandhi.
Savṛṣā, Prajñā, Haṃsā, Prabhā, Varāhī, Niśā, Vimalā, Amoghā,
Narasiṃhavidyutā, and Praṇigaditā are the Śaktis joined with their forms [as the Halas].
Having uttered the syllables together with the half-moons, one should place the forms ending in *śakti* and *ṅe*, followed by *namas*.
Then, having spoken [the mantras] beginning with *ya*, one should assign the seven constituents (*dhātu*), as well as *prāṇa*, *śakti*, and *krodha*, to the self.
I worship Viṣṇu, whose splendor is like that of a hundred rising suns, who is as radiant as molten gold, who is attended on both sides by the Daughter of the Ocean and the Mother of the Universe,
who is adorned with various ornaments glittering with diverse jewels, and who wears yellow garments.
[He saw him] holding a lotus, the Kaumodakī mace, and a discus in his hands.
Having thus meditated upon the Supreme Person, he who should perform the nyāsa with the syllables joined by the names Keśava and the others, day by day,
shall for a long time be augmented with intelligence, longevity, memory, fortitude, beauty, fame, prosperity, and good fortune.
That wise man who follows this very rite preceded by Ramā shall attain the vast earth;
furthermore, at the end, he goes to the state of Hari.

Thus, having made his body imperishable, he should perform the deposition of the principles (tattvanyāsa), preceded by the syllable *ma* and followed by the supreme syllable (*parākṣara*) and the word of salutation (*namas*).

Furthermore, he should successively utter the mantras of the principles, ending with the word of salutation, for the Supreme (*para*), for that which is called "that" (*tadāhvaya*), and for the Self (*ātman*).

Having joined the individual soul (*jīva*) and the vital breath (*prāṇa*) within the entire body, the practitioner should place the intellect (*mati*), ego (*ahaṅkāra*), and mind (*manas*) in the center. Then,
he should place the group of qualities (*guṇagaṇa*) preceded by sound (*śabda*) in the mouth, heart, private parts, and feet, as well as those situated in the ears and other locations.
Preceded by hearing.
Upon the dissolution of the group of organs beginning with speech into the Self, one should contemplate the series starting with space [in the locations] of the head,

mouth, heart, throat, and feet; and the solar, lunar, and fiery orbs, which are pervaded by twelve, sixteen, eight, four, and ten digits respectively, situated in the heart-lotus and within the heart.
The knower of mantras [should recite] with the syllables *bhū*, *va*, *su*, *mu*, *nya*, *kṣya*, and *kṣa*.
Then, one should assign the Upaniṣads— namely *parameṣṭhin*, *pumān*, *viśvanivṛtti*, and *sarva*—
to the locations beginning with space (*ākāśa*) and so forth, using the syllables *ya*, *ra*, *la*, *va*, and *la*, together with the nasal bindu (*la-vaka*).
Vāsudeva, Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, Aniruddha,
and Nārāyaṇa are considered, in sequence, to be identical with Parameṣṭhin and the others.
Then, the knower of that [truth] should place the essence of *kopa* (wrath), joined with the *kṣāra* (the letter *kṣa*) and the *indu* (the nasal bindu), as Nṛsiṃha upon all the limbs in due order;
thus is described the deposition (*nyāsa*) consisting of the *tattvas*, which brings about the close presence [of the deity] in the Viśvamūrti and other forms.
When this has been done, he certainly becomes authorized in all Vaiṣṇava rites, such as the recitation of mantras;
by means of this [initiation], he may practice the restraint of breath (prāṇāyāma) here, desiring to recite the mantra.

Alternatively, in all procedures for the recitation of Hari’s mantras, one should practice the restraint of the breaths through the root mantra according to the prescribed method, repeating it as many times as there are principles (tattvas). Furthermore,
that triad [of breath-restraints] is ordained by the wise to be performed both before and after the recitation.
He who performs this sixteen-fold [rite] here day by day is indeed purified from great sin within a month;
or else, for all rites of chanting the name of Kṛṣṇa, there is excellent self-restraint through the mantra born of the limbs.
One should practice it seven times in conjunction with the [mantra] that removes all evils.
One of highly praised intellect, while reciting the twenty-eight-syllable mantra that bestows desired fruits, should restrain the breath; or, if using the eighteen-syllable mantra,
one should practice on Sundays, reciting other mantras according to their syllables, performing exhalation (recaka) and inhalation (pūraka).
A man who is highly skilled [should practice] the application of the vital breath.
One should exhale through the *dakṣā* [nāḍī] with the right [nostril], fill [the lungs] through the *vāmā* with the left, and then retain [the breath] through the central channel (*madhyamā nāḍī*).
This is declared to be the triad beginning with exhalation (*recaka*), known as *kalā*, *daṇḍa*, and *vidyā*, consisting of measured durations (*mātrā*).

Having performed *prāṇāyāma*, one should then fashion the *yogapīṭha* with one's own body; one should install [upon it] the foundational power (*ādhāraśakti*), primordial nature (*prakṛti*), the seat of action (*karmaṭha*), the serpent Śeṣa, the earth, the ocean of milk, the White Island (*śvetadvīpa*), the great pavilion honored and radiant with jewels, and the wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpavṛkṣa*).
Furthermore, [he is placed] in the region of the heart, in the two shoulders, the two thighs, the two faces, the two hips, and the pair of sides.
One should place *dharma* and so forth, as well as *adharma* and so forth, upon the four limbs and members; then, in the heart, the remainder of the lotus.
One should place the Sun, Moon, and Fire, conjoined with the parts of the *praṇava*, along with the initial syllables of their names, representing *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*.

Having first placed the triad beginning with the Self (ātman) together with its seed-syllables, and then having placed the Knower of the Field (jñānātman) using the syllables of space (vyoma), fire (agni), and māyā, one should place the nine Śaktis— eight in the directions around the center and one in the middle— and then duly place the Pīṭha-mantra there, situated in the center of its pericarp.
One should contemplate that immortal abode, which is the light of eternal bliss and consciousness.
The powers (śaktis) are Vimalā, Utkarṣiṇī, Jñānā, Kriyā, Yogā, Prahvī,
Satyā, Īśānā, and the ninth is remembered as Anugrahā.
The syllable *tāram* is the heart-mantra; the Lord Viṣṇu, the soul of all beings, is accompanied by all [mantras].
The forms of Vāsudeva ending in the neuter suffix *-am* are joined with the Soul of All (*sarvātman*). This is the conjunction.
At the conclusion of yoga, the essence of the lotus-seat (padmapīṭha) is joined with the feminine suffix (ṅī), and at the end, the syllable *nati* is added;
this mantra, declared as the beloved of the seat, is sufficient for all ritual services.
Having made the pair of hands consist of the mantra, one should perform everything by means of these two according to the path that will be described,
using the syllables of the mantra for that supreme and unsurpassed light of Hari.
Thus ends the first chapter of the Kramadīpikā.
I shall declare the mantra, whose majesty is renowned throughout the three worlds and which is sought after by sages possessing an inexhaustible store of merit.
It has as its object the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa), bestows wealth, virtue, desire, and liberation, and is expert in all magical rites (*kārmaṇa*).

This most secret [teaching] is like a fire to a heap of cotton for those who lack understanding; it bestows the sovereignty of speech upon men, removes misfortune, and is the sole cause for warding off the afflictions of poison, untimely death, malevolent planets, and disease.
It bestows victory in battle, grants fearlessness in the forest, and provides easy crossing during a flood;
it increases men, horses, chariots, and elephants, and brings forth sons, cattle, land, wealth, and grain.

What more need be said of that which bestows strength, heroism, valor, splendor, radiant beauty, and charm; which agitates millions of cosmic eggs; and which grants the eightfold qualities such as the power of becoming minute? It is the giver of everything.
The syllable *śā* is the wielder of the Śārṅga bow; *rṅgī* is the one with an upper tooth; *śū* is the hero;

*ro* is the one joined with the left eye; *va* is the second letter; *mā* is the trident-bearer; *kṣi* is Viṣṇu; *yu* is the child; *k* is the pair following Balarāma; and these constitute the four syllables.
The fourth [syllable] should be *śūra*, followed by *sānanavṛtta*; the seventh and eighth should be *agnisakha*.
Then, taking the pair of syllables that are its beloved (*taddayitākṣarayugma*) and placing them above, one should thus extract the mantra.
This ten-syllable mantra of the Enemy of Madhu has been revealed by you;
it especially increases devotion to His pair of lotus feet.
The sage Nārada is proclaimed as its seer (ṛṣi), and the Virāṭ meter is declared by the sages;
the deity is said to be the son of Nandagopa, the bringer of auspiciousness to all the worlds.

The five limbs [of the mantra] were declared by him who is endowed with the power to protect the three worlds, preceded by the one named Asurāntaka, and accompanied by wheels joined with the beloved of the eater of oblations (Agni), well-suited for the functions of his mouth, and arranged according to their grammatical case endings.

If the five limbs are recited with "namaḥ" at the heart, "svāhā" (the beloved of Agni) at the head, "vaṣaṭ" at the crest, "hūm" at the shield, and "phaṭ" as the weapon, and if "vauṣaṭ" is uttered for the two eyes along with the fourth [syllable]: namaḥ hṛdayāya svāhā śirase vaṣaṭ śikhāyai hūm kavacāya pharaṭ astrāya vauṣaṭ netratrayāya.
The ten colors are said to be endowed with ten mantra-syllables and crescent moons,
ending with the word "namas.
Following that are the heart, head, crest, armor, weapon, and the two flanks.
The back of the cart is joined upwards.

I shall declare the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of this mantra: the letter *Śa* (Śakrī) conjoined with the wheel of power (*śakti-cakra*) and illuminated by the left eye (*vāmanetra*), together with *Pra* and *Dyumna*.
This is declared to be the seed-syllable; this is the Prādyumna-mantra, which deludes the world.
The *haṃsa* (the letter *ha*) is endowed with the rounded belly of fat (*meda*); that *potrī* (the letter *ra*), joined with the eyes and so forth (*netrādi*), consists of four syllables (*yugārṇā*).
This is declared to be the *śakti* of Agni, who is worshipped by all the hosts of gods; it is the beloved of Agni and bestows the fulfillment of desires.
The application of this mantra is for the four aims of human life;
Kṛṣṇa is said to be the material cause (prakṛti), and Durgā is the presiding deity.
She protects all this, and she protects the Supreme Person; thus, "Gopī" is Prakṛti. That which is born from her is "Gopījana," meaning the series beginning with Mahat and ending with Earth.
Because he pervades these two—the Gopīs and the Jana—by being their support through the wind (the vital breath), he is taught to be the "Vallabha" (Beloved).
The light that is dense bliss and stainless.
" Svāhā! I cause my own self to go [to Him]!"—thus, for that one who is the Lord of cause and effect, the Supreme Self, there shall be non-falling unity with Acyuta.
Alternatively, "gopījana" refers to the collective assembly of powers capable of protecting the entire world.
Its own non-different master is designated here as the Beloved (Vallabha).
Or else, thinking "I offer even this which is mine to my beloved of the young women of Vraja," one should offer everything into the Saguna Brahman for the sake of all prosperity. || 1 ||

The word *kṛṣi* has the meaning of "existence," and *na* signifies "the nature of bliss"; therefore, he is *Kṛṣṇa*. Furthermore, because he draws away (*karṣaṇa*) the sins of his devotees and because his body consists of mantra which possesses that [same] color, he is *Kṛṣṇa*. Since *go* denotes sound, it is knowledge; because he is perceived through that, he is *Govinda*.
Govinda knows the multitude of words; he has not been mentioned even because of his investigation.

These [syllables] are placed in order in the presence [of the deity], according to the division of the musical instrument (tūrya): first before the mantra, then from the seed-syllable of Manmatha, and afterwards.

If this most excellent mantra of eighteen syllables, the secret of secrets and the wish-fulfilling gem for all desires, is [practiced], the virtuous maintain that its deity is the Sage (Brahmā) as previously ordained and its meter is Gāyatrī.
Its limbs consist of four syllables each, ending with the armor (*varman*), while the weapon (*astra*) consists of two syllables.
The seed-syllable, the power, the nature, and the application of this [mantra] are as before;
now I shall describe the placement (nyāsa) of the preceding one, which brings about all accomplishments, according to the desire of the mind.
The sword is placed across the two hands on the inner and outer sides, its tip restrained by the *tāra*.
The placement (*nyāsa*) should be performed with the phonemes situated between pairs of *tāras*, adorned with *bindus*, for the sake of the rites of the Heart.

On the branches [of the hands], a person of clear intellect should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of three joints separately on each of the ten fingers, beginning with the right thumb and ending with the left thumb; this is declared to be the *sṛṣṭi* (emission) performed upon the hands.
The *sthiti* (maintenance) begins with the pair of thumbs on both hands, while the *saṃhṛti* (withdrawal) begins with the left [thumb].
This triad, situated near the right thumb, also brings forth the effect endowed with persistence.
Then, according to the sequence of placement, the wise one should assign the ten limbs;
likewise, the procedure for the five limbs on the hand has been declared.
O Lord of Men, having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) with the letters of the Mātṛkā accompanied by the bindu and preceded by the mantra, as before.
And the ten principles, O knower of the colors of the mantras, arise from the distinction between the paths of withdrawal and emanation.
The best of men, having withdrawn and followed along, may encounter an obstruction on the path of emanation;
indeed, their extraction is as previously described, and now I shall explain the rite of ritual placement (nyāsa).
Earth, water, fire, air, ether, ego, intellect, primordial nature (*prakṛti*), and spirit (*puruṣa*)—these are the principles (*tattva*).
Among these, five are located in the feet, anus, heart, mouth, and genitals respectively; two are in the middle [the hands]; and the remaining one is in the entire body.
By way of the opposite of that.
This most secret placement (nyāsa), perfected by the ten principles (tattvas), has been fully described;
it should also be performed by the virtuous upon other Gopālaka mantras for the swift attainment of results.
One should place the supreme mantra, encircled by the *dhruva* (the syllable *oṃ*), three times upon the body from the hair to the feet with both arms;
likewise, one should place the individual syllables on the head, the two eyes, the two ears, the nose, the mouth, the heart, the belly, the genitals, and the knees.

The process of emanation has been described; the wise sages have also declared the process of maintenance, which extends from the heart to the mouth, and the process of reabsorption, which extends from the feet to the head.
One should perform this triad in the order of emanation followed by maintenance.
This placement (nyāsa), ending with reabsorption, is prescribed for the mendicants (maskarin) and forest-dwellers (vaikhānasa).
They say that for householders, [the cycle] ends with maintenance, while for those in the stages of life (varṇins), it ends with creation.

Some teachers say that for a householder endowed with dispassion, [the mudrā] is *saṃhāra*; for one who dwells in the forest possessing innate knowledge, it is *sthiti*; and for those seeking learning, it is *sṛṣṭi*. That same [mudrā] which is prescribed at the head is the *madhyā* when placed at the eye together with the index finger.
In the ears, the middle finger is joined with the index finger while the thumbs are excluded;
in the nose and the mouth, all fingers are used; in the heart, the index finger is placed;
in the navel, the middle finger is joined with the first (index) finger; and in the auspicious [forehead], they are placed in the ears.
Those same [syllables], together with the thumbs, are for the two fingers, the two knees, and the two feet;
there is a specific assignment for the locations and the syllables, but not for the individual fingers themselves.
This supreme Nyāsa, called Bhṛtya, is intended for those who speak [the truth];
it bestows prosperity, consists of ten repetitions, and is most secret even from the best of counselors.
[The letters are placed] on the foundation, the forehead, the navel, the heart, the throat, and the mouth;
[and] on the two thighs, the neck and the navel, the belly and the heart, the pair of breasts, the two sides, and the other hip.

In whose eyes, ears, cheeks, hands, feet, joints, fingertips, branches [of the limbs], and in whose eastern and other directions, as well as upon his head, entire arms, and likewise his thighs, [does that splendor reside]?
One should place [the syllables] *sviṇya*, *amarṇān*, and *manūṇyān* upon the head, eyes, mouth, throat, navel, heart, genitals, anus, arms, knees, and feet;
and one should assign them to the ears, cheeks, shoulders, sides, buttocks, and thighs.
In the case of words ending in *jānu*, *jaṅghā*, *aṅghri*, and *yuk*.
Thus has been described the "Cage of Manifestations" (*vibhūtipañjara*), which bestows all happiness, wealth, dharma, and liberation;
it is an ointment for the eyes of young women and increases devotion to the lotus feet of Hari.
Now, for the sake of the manifestation of this mantra, the "Cage of Forms" (*mūrtipañjara*) is proclaimed.
It destroys distress, evil planets, and poison, and bestows fame, prosperity, beauty, and nourishment.

One should sequentially place the twelve syllables of the mantra of Bhava (Śiva), beginning with Keśava and the six forms of the Yugas, starting from Dhātṛ and ending with Mihira, using the vowels excluding the neuter ones.

One should place the mantra of six pairs of syllables on the forehead, the belly, the heart, the pit of the throat, the left and right sides, the ends of the arms, the neck, the three on the left, the back, the crown of the head, and likewise on the top of the head.
Vāsudeva, whose body is the nectar of consciousness and who possesses the brilliance of ten million suns, stands above with his form pervading everything;
he permeates it like pure water sprinkled upon a vessel, filling it with the manifest letters of the mantra.
Having formed the mudrā, one should place the emanation and maintenance [mantras], the pair of fifteen-limbed [mantras], and the triad beginning with the sage-mantra upon the head, heart, and hands.
Furthermore, the ten directions are to be saluted.
*Tāra*, *hārda*, the *viśvamūrti* [mantras], *śārṅgī*, and *māṃsa* at the end of the syllables, with *vāyu* in the middle— these are the excellent deities.
This best of mantras, consisting of twelve syllables, is said to be the direct gateway to the city of liberation.
This is easily understood.
Dhātṛ, Aryaman, Mitra, Varuṇa, Aṃśu, Bhaga, Vivasvat, Indra, Pūṣan,
Parjanya, Tvaṣṭṛ, and Viṣṇu are declared to be the Ādityas (the Suns).
Now, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of the syllables of the mantra, consisting of pairs and single sounds, upon the fixed point (*dhruva*);

then, perform the five-limbed (*pañcāṅga*) placement on the two hands and the five fingers. Having pervaded the body limb by limb, and having placed the *praṇava* three times and once [respectively], the letters of the mantra should then be placed with reverence, followed again by the words.

One of pure intellect should certainly place the protective syllables on the hairline, the two ends of the eyebrows on the forehead, the pair of ears, the two eyes, the face, the neck, the heart, the navel, the hips, both groins, the knees, and the feet; and finally, the syllable *dhruva* (om) on the head.
One should rub the five points—the eyes, heart, secret place, and feet.
One should again perform the placement of the five limbs (pañcāṅga-nyāsa), as well as the sages and so forth;
everything else is the same as before. Now I shall describe the mudrās which belong to the mantras.
The fingers of the hand, straight and without the thumb [extended], form the mudrā for the heart and the head;
the fist with the thumb tucked underneath is indeed for the crest-lock (śikhā); and the fingers of both hands joined together constitute the armor (varma).

The sound produced by the thumbs and index fingers of both arms raised in the *nārāca-muṣṭi* [fist] gesture, which is directed everywhere, is declared to be the *astra-mudrā*; in this case, the eyes are fixed upon the index and middle fingers.
When [the deity] is pleased, the thumb of the left hand is joined to its little finger,
and that little finger is extended while joined with the thumb of the right hand.
The index, middle, and ring fingers slightly contracted and moved [upward]—
this is here called the flute mudrā, well-guarded and the beloved of Hari.
The garland, the Śrīvatsa, and the Kaustubha are not mentioned here because they are already well-known;
however, the Bhadrā, which has the shape of a bilva fruit, is mentioned among the mudrās of Acyuta.
Having raised the left thumb and bound its tip with the thumb of the other hand, and having pressed it with the fingers of that [right hand] as well as the fingers of the left hand,
one of pure intellect should bind [the hands] firmly and place them at the heart while reciting the seed-syllable of Māra known as *vilva*.
This mudrā has been clearly explained here; it should be kept secret by those who know the ritual procedure.
Whatever evil deed one has committed here or in the past, whether intentionally or unintentionally, through mind, speech, or body—
knowing this mudrā, a person destroys it all; the hosts of gods bow down to him, for they are subject to his will.
All people are always [thus].
Having uttered the *sudarśana* mantra— beginning with the *praṇava*, ending with the *hṛdaya*, followed by the word "Sudarśana" in the dative case,
and concluding with the weapon-word (*astra*) and *phaṭ*— one should ward off the ten directions with this mantra using the *astramudrā*.
Having thus described Him who is skilled in the creation, preservation, and destruction of the entire universe,
who is sought by the Vedas, unborn, and possesses a human form— one should remember that Beloved of the cowherd women.
Thus ends the second chapter of the *Kramadīpikā*.
Now, with trees whose branches are bent by clusters of fresh sprouts and blossoming flowers from which honey flows with manifest fragrance;
One of pure intellect should remember the cool and auspicious Vṛndāvana, entwined with graceful, creeping vines bearing blossoming new clusters of flowers.
The interior was made resonant by the humming of bees moving about, sweet with the tasting of the nectar of blossoming flowers;
and it was filled here and there with the cries of birds such as pigeons, parrots, mynas, and cuckoos. The earth—[was thus] made to resound.
Agitated by the dancing of Śakra.

It was incessantly frequented by those intent on tossing about the garments of the playful women of Vraja— garments that were grey with the mass of pollen from the bellies of blossoming lotuses, carried by the spray of the moving waves of the daughter of Kalinda, and which seemed to kindle the passion of the God of Love.
By the Maruts.
With sprouts of coral and fresh shoots, leaves of emerald, clusters of diamond and pearl as its buds, and various fruits of the hue of lotuses;
it is the most massive tree, constantly served by all the seasons, a granter of desires— even within its interior is the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa).
One should contemplate with uplifted joy.
Furthermore, unwearied, he should again meditate upon the golden ground beneath the range of its beautiful golden peaks, radiant with the light of the rising sun,
showering sprays of nectar,
possessing a floor of blazing jewels, and brilliant with heaps of flower-pollen.
The wise one [should contemplate] that which is free from the six waves.
Having meditated upon a red eight-petalled lotus situated upon a most expansive yogic throne set within a jeweled pavement,
one should then contemplate Mukunda seated comfortably in its center, possessing the splendor of the rising sun.

O King, his hair is a mass of very glossy, dark-blue, thick, and curled locks, possessing a luster like a fresh blue lotus or a dense cloud of crushed collyrium; and his crest is adorned with the beautiful peacock feathers of the blue-throated one.
His head was adorned with flowers from the celestial tree, cherished by the playful hands of Rati; he wore fresh blue lotuses as ear-ornaments;
his forehead shone with a mark of yellow pigment (gorocanā) shimmering amidst his flickering locks of hair; and his majesty was radiant with the brilliance of his crown.
His face was as beautiful as the orb of the full autumnal moon; his eyes were wide like lotus petals;
his cheeks were made radiant by the shimmering rays from jeweled makara-shaped earrings; and his nose was high and lovely.
Her lower lip is more beautiful than vermilion; her smile, radiant as the moon, jasmine, and mandāra flowers, illuminates the quarters of the sky;
her neck is charmingly resplendent with a necklace fashioned from a profusion of wild sprouts and blossoms;
and her shoulders are adorned with a hanging garland of santāna flowers frequented by intoxicated, wandering bees.

[He beheld] Him whose thick thighs were adorned by a series of necklaces like the *bhagaṇa* [constellation] shining upon the expanse of the sky; who possessed the luster of the Kaustubha gem as His radiant mantra;
who was marked by the excellent *śrīvatsa* sign; whose shoulders were elevated; and whose well-formed arms were thick, rounded, and reached down to His knees.
With a belly that is deep and without folds, a broad and profound navel, and a line of hair as lovely as a swarm of female bees;
adorned with armlets, bracelets, necklaces, girdles, anklets, and a waist-band all fashioned from various jewels.

His limbs were stained with divine unguents; his hips were encircled by a yellow garment; his beautiful thighs, knees, and well-proportioned, lovely shanks were visible; the beauty of his lovely, elevated forefeet surpassed that of the tortoise;
and his lotus-like feet were made beautiful by toenails shining like rubies and jewel-encrusted rings upon his toes.
It was beautiful with the soles of its redder feet marked by the fish, the goad, the lotus, the banner, the swastika, and the thunderbolt.
[He beholds her] whose bodily beauty—composed of a collection of the very essence of loveliness—reproaches the splendor of the body of the Mind-born God (Kāma);
and [he beholds her] with divine melodies set in motion by the fingers of her trembling hand as they fill the holes of the flute at her lotus-like mouth.
It was surrounded by cows whose continuous lineages of offspring had been eternally melted away, forming an infinite ocean of mouths;
whose eyes were dissolved into their lotus-like faces; who moved slowly and heavily, stumbling under the weight of their udders;
and whose tails, like creepers, were raised up while they held the remaining tips of grass-stalks between their teeth.
And by the young calves, who were charming with their mouths fixed motionless as they sucked the teats from which milk flowed, and whose ears were pricked up to listen to the enchanting,
slow songs produced by the flute; And by the young deer, who had their ears raised high to hear the lovely, slow melodies set forth on the flute.

With herds of young bulls and heifers whose hooves were tossed about in the excitement of leaping and striking with soft heads against fresh horns, and who were drenched with moisture from their thick dewlaps and uplifted tails;
With great bulls, though large, distressed by the weight of their massive humps, shaking the circle of the quarters with their lowing cries,
and possessing broad nostrils opened wide as they drank the nectar of the sound of the bamboo flute from the hollows of their upturned ears;
Accompanied by cowherds whose appearance, conduct, age, and dress were identical to his own, who played flutes and lutes with a swelling and melodious sound,
who were intent on singing with slow and high rhythmic beats, and who were skilled in performing graceful dances with their swaying vine-like arms.
It was surrounded by playful children whose calves were thick at the ends and whose broad hips were bound with rows of dangling tinkling bells that jingled as they moved;
who wore neck-ornaments fashioned from the claws of hyenas; and who spoke with indistinct yet charming voices.

Then, there were the beautiful cowherd girls, moving slowly under the weight of their broad hips and heavy buttocks; their bodies bore the lines of the three folds of skin and the rising line of hair, bent by the burden of their full breasts;
and their limbs and feet were made to blossom by the nectar-like essence of the exceedingly beautiful and charming music of his flute.
Their creeper-like bodies were adorned with the rising of horripilation, beautiful as the unfolding of flower buds.
Thus, from the ocean of the waters of passion, which was made to blossom by the moonlight of the beautiful smile of the tree [of youth],
there issued forth continuous streams of drops of perspiration, equal to the spray from the breaking of most tremulous waves.
By the rain of Cupid’s sharp arrows— discharged from his exceedingly beautiful bow of eyebrows—
their entire vital organs were shattered, and their limbs, overwhelmed by it, were pervaded by the pain of unbearable trembling.
For those who are longing for the act of drinking the nectar-essence of the beauty of that exceedingly lovely and charming form.
Of those whose lotus-eyes were languidly tremulous, carrying a flood of the waters of affection.
[The women] were attended for a moment by swarms of bees greedy for honey, which flowed from the blossoming flowers falling from their loosened braids;
they spoke with soft voices faltering from the intoxication and passion of Māra, while their girdles swayed and their waist-knots became slack.
Of those whose splendor of their hips was revealed by the ends of fine Chinese silken garments.
Of those whose faces fill the quarters with the tinkling of jeweled anklets produced by the gentle pressure of their feet, lovely upon the surface of the floor;
and whose lotus-like eyes, thick with lashes, have their petal-like lips quivering.
Of those wearing shimmering earrings.
Of those whose sprout-like lower lips were withered by the heat of the wind from their longest sighs.
Constantly attended on all sides by rows of lotus-hands shimmering with various means (upāya).
He bore [the form] whose entire body was filled with garlands of full-blown blue lotuses— their long, tremulous, dark eyes— and which was the locus of manifold amorous graces;
he bore it as it tasted the honey dripping from the charming lotus-faces of those women.
A captivating garland of bees, which are her eyes intoxicated by the dissolution [of the world].
Outside this [mandala], one should visualize in front of it a host of deities led by Brahmā, Śiva, and Indra, consisting of cowherd women, cowherds, and cattle,
who are intent on offering hymns of praise and seeking wealth.

Similarly, on the right [side], he saw a multitude of sages intent on the traditional teachings (āmnāya) out of a desire for wealth and dharma; and behind Yogīndranātha, those such as Sanaka and others who, desiring liberation, were established in meditative absorption (samādhi).
On the left, he saw yakṣas, siddhas, gandharvas, vidyādharas, and cāraṇas,
along with kinnaras and the foremost apsarases, all seeking sensual pleasures and engaged in dancing, singing, and instrumental music.
[He is] white as a conch, the moon, or a kunda flower; he knows all the scriptures; his mass of matted hair is tawny like a flash of lightning;
and he desires unwavering devotion directed toward his lotus feet, having utterly abandoned all other attachments.

One should meditate upon that son of the Creator, the lord of sages, in the sky, who delights [the world] with enchanting modulations (*mūrcchanās*) belonging to the three scales (*grāmas*) of the seven notes, which are endowed with the qualities of various kinds of musical intervals (*śruti*). He gladdens them with these exalted melodies.

Having thus meditated upon himself as the son of Nanda, one of sharp and clear intellect should worship him with blameless offerings such as water for the feet (*arghya*) and so forth, visualizing him before his mind;
furthermore, one should worship with devotion by means of external riches within one's own body— this we declare to be the procedure.
And may we now [attain] that which bestows incomparable proximity.
Having swept his own sacrificial ground on the earth with cow-dung and water,
and having placed a vessel there, he, established in his position, should purify the conch with water using the weapon-mantra.
There, one should cast perfumes, *sumanā* flowers, and unbroken rice grains while reciting the heart-mantra;
then, the wise one should fill it with pure water using the syllables of the mantra, beginning from the end and proceeding back toward the head-syllable.

In the seats, the conch, and the waters, one who knows the mantra should worship the mandalas of the Fire, the Day-maker (Sun), and the Night-maker (Moon) in sequence with the syllables of the poison-mantra, preceded by the [syllable of] the face.
There, one should cause the sacred water (tīrtha) to flow from the orb of the hot-rayed sun [into the vessel] by means of the Anunā mantra;
likewise, one should extract it from one's own heart-lotus and display the Gālinī mudrā with the Śikhā mantra.
Having gazed upon that water with the eye-mantra and having covered it with the armor-mantra while joined by both arms,
one should assign it as the totality through the root-mantra and the limbs, and protect the directions with the weapon-mantra.
Touching the water mixed with unbroken grains (*akṣata*) and other substances that has been made *acyuta*, he should recite the mantra eight times;
he should then cast a little into the water of the *vardhanī* vessel and sprinkle his own body with it.

In this manner, one should perform the entire preparation of flowers, sandalwood, and so forth three times with the *manu* "kareṇa. This secret method, which concludes with the filling of the conch, is proclaimed here as the foremost of all sacrificial rites.
O Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Godāvarī, Sarasvatī, Narmadā, Sindhu, and Kāverī, be present in these waters!
This Tīrthamanu has been proclaimed as the dispeller of the flood of misdeeds.
The little fingers and thumbs of the two hands are joined to one another;
the index, middle, and ring fingers are held together, straight, and unbent.
This is declared to be the Gālinī mudrā, performed above the conch.
Then, having worshipped one's own lords and Gaṇanāyaka in the center of the mūla-cakra at the crown of the head,
and by means of the seat-mantras (pīṭha-mantra) according to the sequence of ritual placement, [one should worship] with water, sandalwood paste, unbroken rice, flowers, incense, and lamps.
Then, one should offer oblations at the root of the radiance of the root-mantra, at the heart, and in the middle of the earth;
for one who contemplates this triad as unified, it appears like a flash of lightning, a mass of bliss.

Having made that fire possessed of limbs by means of its constituent parts, and having performed the placement (nyāsa) up to the end of the limbs with the *vibhūti* mantra, the practitioner of mantras should worship it with offerings beginning with the seat (*āsana*) and ending with ornaments,
and further perform the ritual worship with water, scents, and so forth, according to the procedure for the limbs starting with the *ātṛpti* offering.
Furthermore, one should place the flute in his mouth, the forest garland upon his chest,
and offer the Śrīvatsa mark and the Kaustubha jewel above his breasts.

Then, having anointed her limbs with the flow of sandalwood paste, she should draw auspicious marks on her forehead and other parts with the root-mantra; thereafter, being free from ailment, she should draw figures shaped like lamp-flames using the mantras of the Pañjara-mūrtis.
Then one should spread a handful of flowers: with the root mantra five times at the pair of feet,
with two *tulasī* leaves in the middle, with two *hayāri* (bilva) leaves on the head, with two *padma* (lotus) leaves over the entire body with the six [mantras],
and finally with all [the mantras] over the whole body.
White flowers, smeared with white sandalwood paste, are on the right side; red flowers, sprinkled with red sandalwood paste, are on the left side.
Likewise, having offered incense and lamps, one should gratify Kṛṣṇa with nectar-like juices;
then, having offered mouth-perfume, one should worship him with fragrant flowers and other offerings.
Having gratified [the deity] with betel, song, dance, and instrumental music,
the practitioner of mantra should perform the offering of his own self with a mouthful of water while reciting the mantra known as *brahmārpaṇa*.
Alternatively, for those of contracted intellects, this ritual has been proclaimed as commenced with a cage of images,
consisting of six, eighteen, and thirty-six syllables, along with its own phonemes, words, and limbs, preceded by the flute.
Meditating single-mindedly upon the son of Mathananda, who is supremely serene, one should recite the mantra;
and upon completing the prescribed number of recitations according to the rule while maintaining mindfulness of its purpose, one should perform the concluding rite.
Having heated the seed-syllable enclosed by the *praṇava* one hundred and eight times, the high-minded practitioner should apply the yogas obtained from the mouth of his own guru; then,
being of the nature of the eternally real consciousness-bliss (*sad-anṛta-cid-ānanda-ātman*), he should offer the recitation— thus is the complete procedure for recitation.
It is declared to be based on two mantras.
The man who follows this method will become beloved by all embodied beings;
indeed, even if he is merely a temple for a single lotus-like speech, in the end he attains that supreme splendor.
Thus ends the third chapter of the Śrī Kramadīpikā.
Indeed, the practice of mantra is said to be the means for accomplishing all perfections—
that by performing which the sages, such as Nārada and others, attained the greatest perfection in this world.

He who [honored] that Brahmin— who had crushed the host of his enemies beginning with Pradhava, whose limbs were stainless, who bore a profound devotion characterized by a passion for the dust of the pair of Kṛṣṇa’s lotus feet,
who was a knower of the pure paths of the Vedas, Śāstras, and Āgamas, and who was honored among the virtuous and self-controlled— [with knowledge].
Desiring to understand thoroughly, one whose mind and body are inclined toward it should take refuge in a teacher.
With a heart that is straightforward and exceedingly tender, he should satisfy the Guru with his own wealth, even if it be meager, and with agreeable speech.
For three years, being extremely steadfast, he should speak with the thought that the Guru is the Lotus-navelled Lord (Viṣṇu), for the sake of the Guru’s satisfaction.
Now, the initiation (dīkṣā) celebrated in the *Prapañcasāra* is briefly recalled here for the attainment of all perfections.
Without which, even for one who is constantly engaged in recitation, the multitude of mantras will not grant success.
Then, the wise man should, according to the prescribed rite, prepare a site on a plot of ground and offer the sacrificial oblation (vāstu-bali) to the deities of the dwelling;
thereafter, he should construct a pavilion there, measuring eight cubits in length and provided with a smooth altar.
It was encircled by a garland of kuśa grass joined with threads of the three qualities (guṇas), adorned with the banner of primordial nature (prakṛti),
featuring four faces as its water-born arches, and shining brightly, resplendent with a white canopy.
In this [mandala],

let the wise one establish the seat of the Lord of Wealth (Vasupati) in the eastern direction, with a pit eight fingers deep and wide; it should have eight girdles and four corners representing the eight Vasus.
It is characterized by a yoni that measures the size of the cheek of an elephant standing facing west.
Then, in the pavilion sprinkled with cow-fragrant water, one should properly draw the mandala as an eight-petaled lotus,
complete with three circles, the seat of the zodiac signs, the pedestals, the walkways, the four gates, the primary and secondary ornaments,
and the splendors. Then the preceptor, knowing the ritual procedure, having performed the preliminary ablutions and the rites up to the self-worship;
In front of his own left [hand], he should also place a conch shell and vessels filled with water for the arghya, pādya, ācamana, and other rites.
Having placed flowers, scents, unbroken rice, and so forth elsewhere, and having also placed a vessel behind for the washing of the hands.
When everything else has been illuminated by the rows of lamps within the range of one's own vision, one should perform the ritual means (*sādhana*).
First, the row of seats extending from the northwest to the northeast should be honored;
elsewhere as well, the son of Ambikā (Gaṇeśa) is to be worshipped, holding a noose, a tusk, a goad, and the gesture of fearlessness in his lotus-like hands.

Having worshipped the feet of the gods beginning with Ādhāraśakti, one should then worship Dharma and the other [qualities] in the middle portion located in the directions of Fire, Rakṣas, Wind, and Śiva, as well as Adharma and the others in the intermediate directions; in the center,
one should worship the remaining lotus-disk triad consisting of the qualities and the collection of qualities, and in the midst of the filaments, in each respective place.
And one should not worship the Śaktis again with the Pīṭha-mantra.

Then, one should place rice in the center, along with pure lotuses and the finest grains of husked rice; upon those, one should place *darbha* grass together with *kūrca* bundles and unbroken rice (*akṣata*).
Thereafter, one should place the ten digits (*kalā*) of Fire in clockwise order, beginning with the syllable *ṣa*, and perform the worship.
With fragrant substances and the like,

one should place these [offerings] there; one should set down the *kunta* (spear), which is wound with triple-stranded cotton threads, accompanied by recitation (*japa*), the spreading [of the mandala], and well-perfumed with incense made of *joṅgaka*.

Then, having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) with the pairs of letters beginning with *ka-bha* and ending with *ṭha-ḍa-va-si* upon this spear, one should worship it; thereafter, the twelve digits (*kalā*) of the sun should be worshipped.
Having thus conceived the fire as the supporting form and the sun likewise as the form of the pitcher,
the knower of the ritual should place upon it a *kūrca* made of gold, joined with unbroken rice and other materials, and radiant with the finest gems.
Then, he should fill it with decoction-water using the letters beginning with *kṣa* and ending with *a*.

At the conclusion of reciting his own mantra three times, he should likewise perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the sixteen digits of the moon— beginning with the group of deities starting with Sṛṣṭi— into this water in the pitcher using milk, the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), or pure water alone. Thereafter,
he should worship those lunar digits with fragrant water, unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), and flowers.
Udīcyā, kuṣṭha, kuṅkuma, ambu, lohasaja, jaṭāmāṃsī, and murā— these,
when well-cooled, are declared to be the "Eight Fragrances" (aṣṭagandha) dear to Hari.
Having thoroughly stirred the eight fragrant substances according to the ritual rule within the interior filled with decoction water,
one should apply the portions of the Moon, Sun, and Fire separately to the service-activity in due order.

The Kalās arising from those respective syllables are produced by the letters beginning with *ka* and ending with *ṭha*; those born from the letter *u* are produced by the letters beginning with *pa* and ending with *ma*; those born from the *bindu* are produced by the letters beginning with *la* and ending with *pa*; and those born from the *nāda* are produced by the group of vowels beginning with *a*.
From the conclusion of the invocation until the final stabilization, the wise one should mutter the respective verses at each stage;
having worshipped each of those [deities] individually, he should duly offer that water into the pitcher with the root mantra.
May the water-pot be covered with clusters of *sahakāra*, *bodhi*, and *panasa* flowers entwined with *śatamanyu* vines, and filled with auspicious circular designs made of flowers, fruits, and rice.
Thereafter, the wise one should wrap the mouth of the jar with a pair of fresh, pure cloths;
and having adorned it here with flowers and other offerings, he should invoke the supreme light.
Having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa upon this Lord Hari residing in the water-pot by means of the sequential placement of the mantras of the elements and principles (tattvas),
the Guru, being attentive, should then worship Him along with His retinue using the various sets of ritual offerings (upacāras).
Having offered a seat and uttered words of welcome, he likewise offers the arghya, pādya, and ācamanīya waters.
First, the Madhuparka offerings, joined with the water for sipping (ācamana), were to be given to the son of Nanda.
Having offered the bath, garments, and ornaments to that [deity] together with his limbs,
the practitioner should then worship his body according to the prescribed ritual procedure with purificatory substances, perfumes, and flowers.
Having first worshipped the primary deities— the pair of arms representing creation and maintenance, the flute, the garland, and the two excellent emblems—
with the root mantra as if performing self-worship, one should then worship the surrounding retinues.
Then, in the directions, Dāma, Sudāma, Vasudāma, and Kiṅkiṇī are to be worshipped;
likewise, one should sacrifice to the external limbs, which consist of radiant forms, upon the filaments.
Another [practitioner] purifies, in sequence, from the heart up to the armor (varma) in the directions of Agni, Nirṛti, Vāyu, and Śiva,
and then the weapon (astra) in the directions starting from the East, using perfumes and other offerings.

The goddesses who preside over the limbs (aṅgadevatās) should be remembered: they possess the luster of a released moonstone, a blue water-lily, a sapphire, and fire; their bodies are preeminent, and their hands quiver as they grant the boons of fearlessness and excellence. Thereafter, one should worship the eight principal queens, beginning with Rukmiṇī, upon the petals.
Their other hands are sealed by holding a beautiful vessel filled with lotuses and wealth in their right hands.
Rukmiṇī, Satyabhāmā, Agnimitrā, Sunandā,
and furthermore Mitravindā, Sulakṣmaṇā, Jāmbavatī, and Suśīlā.

These women possess the luster of refined gold and emeralds, are clad in pure white and variegated garments, have limbs languid from the weight of their full breasts, and are adorned with ornaments resplendent with clusters of various jewels.
Then, one should worship Vasudeva and Devakī,
Nandagopa and Yaśodā, as well as Balabhadra and Subhadrā, upon the tips of the petals.
The cowherd and the cowherdesses have their minds and eyes dissolved in Govinda;
the parents, yellow and pale-white respectively, hold the gesture of knowledge and the gesture of fearlessness in their hands.
Furthermore, the two Mothers, adorned with divine garlands, garments, ointments, and ornaments,
hold a vessel filled with milk-rice (pāyasa) and grant boons;
they are crimson and dark blue respectively, and are embellished with necklaces and jeweled earrings.
Vala, white as a conch or the moon, bearing a mace and a plow,
intoxicated by wine, clad in blue garments, and wearing a single earring with effortless ease.
Dark as a pea, auspicious, most beautiful, adorned with auspicious ornaments, she bestows boons and fearlessness; clad in yellow garments, she is mounted in the prime of youth.
The cowherd boys and girls held in their hands flutes, lutes, cane-staves, conchs, horns, and other instruments,
with their lotus-like hands busy offering various gifts.
And outside of that, one should worship the wish-fulfilling trees (kalpapādapa),
known as Mandāra, Santānaka, Pārijātaka, and Kalpadruma, as well as Haricandana—
trees which are uniquely skilled in granting desired objects and whose branches are bowed down with fruit, situated in the four directions in the center.

One of pure intellect should worship Hari, Havyavāha (Agni), Taraṇija (Sūrya), Kṣapāṭapa (Candra), Pāmpati (Varuṇa), Vāyu, Soma, Śiva, Śeṣa, and Padmaja in their respective directions, accompanied by their respective caste-lords, weapons, vehicles, and retinues.
Indra and the other gods are of various colors— tawny, brown, blue, dark, white, smoky, pure black, bright, and red;
they possess divine attire and are enriched with ornaments shimmering from a multitude of diverse jewels, while their own weapons shine upon their lotus-like hands.
The [deities] named Dambholi, Śakti, Daṇḍa, Kṛpāṇa, Pāśa, Caṇḍāṅkuśa,

Gadā, Triśikha, Vipadma, and others are to be worshipped externally, joined with their own well-marked crowns, and with their lotus-hands raised holding their respective weapons and the gesture of granting fearlessness (abhaya).
In this world, they shine in succession with the luster of gold, silver, water, clouds, emerald, ruby, snow, sapphire, coral, and sprouts;
and by their radiance, they possess wonderful ointments, garments, garlands, and ornaments beginning with diamonds.
Thus has been described the sevenfold enclosure in the ritual for the worship of Acyuta, which brings all happiness;
or else, one may perform this threefold enclosure with the deities beginning with Aṅga, Purandara, and Aśani.

Having thus worshipped with water, flowers, and perfumes, the wise man should then perform the worship of Kṛṣṇa using the eight names of Kṛṣṇa; I shall now declare those names, beginning with "Tārā" and ending with "Namaḥ."
He is Śrī Kṛṣṇa, Vāsudeva, and he who is called Nārāyaṇa;
he is the son of Devakī, the best of the Yadus, and also known as Vārṣṇeya.
At the end of the word *asurākrānta*, the seventh [name] is *bhārahārī*;
and these eight, ending in the dative case, are in order the establishers of the Dharma.
Alternatively, wise persons who have crossed the ocean of worldly existence should perform the worship of the enemy of Kaṃsa with these very [offerings] for the attainment of all desires.
Having prepared incense of thick fragrance from guggulu and other substances— crumbled, mixed with clarified butter, and scattered upon glowing coals—
the mantra-practitioner should offer it low to the Destroyer of the Danujas, while holding the bell with his other hand.
Praising her who was worshipped with perfumes, unbroken grains, and flowers.
With a mind exceedingly clear through vision and other senses, having offered a lamp that rises up with a wick of camphor soaked in fragrant ghee,
reaching as high as the feet,
and having also performed the offering of a handful of flowers and presented the water for the feet (*pādya*) and the water for sipping (*ācamana*), [one should worship].
Then, one of pure intellect should prepare the offering in a golden vessel.
With most fragrant milk-offerings well-boiled, accompanied by side-dishes of white sugar and various beautiful, heart-pleasing flavors;
with curd, fresh butter, new white sugar-candy, sweet cakes, ghee, molasses, coconut, plantains, and the juices of flowers.
Having sprinkled it with water from the [astrological] asterisms and protected it with the seal of the enemy (the *arimudrā*), one should dry it with the fire-element of the right hand;
having incinerated it and filled it with the nectar of the moon from the left hand, one should then consecrate it with the mantra-nectar and, touching it, recite the mantra.
Let him worship Hari, who is completely filled with a hundredfold perfumes from fragrant seals, with offerings of scents;
then, having made a salutation with joined palms, he should pray to Hari and cause the Great Splendor to stream forth from His mouth.
Then, reciting the root mantra ending with "vītihotradayitā," one should pour water;
lifting it up along with flowers, one should offer the oblation consisting of nectar with the *doyuj* mantra.
"I offer this oblation to you; O Hari, may you accept it.
This is the mantra for the offering of the presentation, to be used with one's own name in all forms of worship.
Displaying with the left hand the *prāsa* mudrā, which resembles a full-blown blue lotus,
one should display the *prāṇa* and other [vital winds] with the right hand.
In the first mudrā, one should touch the little finger and the ring finger with the tips of one's own thumbs;
likewise, in the others, the index and middle fingers, as well as the ring and middle fingers, should be positioned in the middle.
The ring finger, the index finger, and the middle finger should be [joined]; likewise, the fourth [finger] with the little finger;
and the fifth should be likewise—thus they are prescribed as the mudrās of the vital breaths and so forth, when conjoined with their respective mantras.
Prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, udāna, and samāna are joined respectively with the fourth [vowel];
ignited by the path of the stars and the support, those mantras therein belong to the black path.
Then, having offered the ring with the principal [mudrā] on both hands,
while touching his own ring finger and reciting his personal mantra, he should display it.
The syllable *na* joined with *ndaja*, *m* with *vu*, *anu* with *vindu*, and *yuṅ*; then *na* with *tiḥ*, *pārśva* with *rāma*, *ru* with *da*, and *vātmanena*;
likewise *ca*, *ruddhaṅe* with *yu*, *taṃ*, *nivedya*, *māṃsa*, *pārśva*, *anila*, and *tathāsiyuk*—[these constitute the mantra].
Having arranged vessels for the seeds and sprouts all around the mandala, the mantra-practitioner should also place lamps made of flour filled with ghee, their flames brightly blazing.
Then, having properly invoked and worshipped Hari into the consecrated fire, he whose mind is pure—
One should offer oblations with milk prepared with white sugar and clarified butter, using white camphor.
Having completed one thousand and eight oblations, one should again present the bali offering to the lords of the zodiac signs,
the lunar mansions, and the karaṇas.
Having prepared the nectar-like water and offered it, having given water for rinsing the mouth and extinguished the fire of the mouth,
having removed the food offering and presented it to Viṣvaksena, and having smeared the ground once again;
Having offered him mouth-rinsing water, tooth-sticks, water for sipping, cleansing of the hands and face, ointments, fragrant mouth-perfumes, garlands, ornaments, and betel-leaf,
and having worshipped him with excellent musical instruments, dance, and song as if he were fully satisfied,
one should then offer him the Arghya water along with his retinue using perfumes and other offerings, and perform the ritual.
Having respectfully offered a handful of flowers and bowed with his head, let him sprinkle himself at the base of His lotus feet with water held in his cupped palms.

Whatever was previously done by me through the authority of the vital breath, the intellect, the body, and the senses, during the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep— whether thought with the mind, spoken with speech, or performed with the two hands, the two feet, the stomach, or the organ of generation— all that becomes an offering to Brahman; Svāhā!
"I offer myself and everything belonging to me completely unto Hari.
Thus is the mantra declared for the surrender of one's own self: "Oṃ tat sat."
Recalling the descent of the nectar from the jar, the wise one should then mutter the mantra one thousand and eight times;
then, having dissolved the coverings within the body of the Conqueror of the Daityas, he should likewise lead even those [coverings] to the nature of nectar.

Having consecrated the sacrificial fire located within the mandala, pavilion, and pit— which has been reached by means of the banner, archway, and water-pitcher— and having worshipped it with flowers at the pitcher, one should again recite the mantra one hundred and eight times.
Then, having fasted as a disciple, at dawn, having performed his daily rites, wearing clean white garments and fine attire,
he should gratify the best of Brahmins with gifts of land, wealth, grain, cows, and herds of cattle for the satisfaction of Lord Hari.
Having circumambulated once more and prostrated before that Teacher, the Supreme Person who possesses a body,
the wise man, having abandoned any stinginess regarding wealth, should offer that sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) and surrender his own subtle body.
Then, once he is comfortably seated upon his throne in the consecration pavilion,

the teacher of pure intellect should first purify him through the rites of drying and so forth; having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) upon his body up to the conclusion of the seat-assignment (pīṭhanyāsa), he should then perform it upon his sword.
Having worshipped with mantras and placed it upon a mark of yellow pigment (rocanā) together with dūrvā grass,

unbroken rice, and flowers, he— surrounded and confident— should bring that water-pot near him, accompanied by the blessings of the twice-born, the clear and resonant sounds of songs and musical instruments, and auspicious rites.

Then, filling his body with the supreme splendor of that deep-blue jewel and great medicinal herb— which partakes of the nature of the highest nectar— he sprinkled him with that state of aesthetic fusion (sāmarasya) in the proper manner.
His body was completely filled with the letters beginning with *ka* and ending with *ha*, while the syllables of the mantra were recited three times;
he wore two very white garments, remained silent, and had performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*).
Having prostrated many times before the one named Deśika Hari and then having touched his feet in salutation,
the disciple sat upon his right side, facing him with a one-pointed mind.
Having duly performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) upon him with scents, unbroken grains (*akṣata*), and other offerings, and having thus adorned his armor,
the Guru should then properly whisper the supreme mantra— endowed with its seer (*ṛṣi*) and other components— three times into his right ear, which is of priceless value.
Having recited the mantra one hundred and eight times as duly consecrated by the Guru,
and having offered salutations, he should then listen properly to the rules of conduct with his body bowed low in devotion.
Having bestowed the mantra upon the disciple and performed the ritual placement (nyāsa), the Guru, having completed the procedure for self-sacrifice,
should recite it one thousand and eight times to avoid any loss of his own spiritual power.
Having offered the entire collection of vessels, such as the water-pots and so forth, to the preceptor, one should then feed the most excellent of the twice-born with various kinds of food.
Those who perform the consecration here according to this rite are indeed blessed; they are the very abode of prosperity and are truly well-favored.
Having spoken this briefly for the sake of recollection by those of clear intellect,
the practitioner of mantra, having entered into this [initiation], should mutter, offer oblations, and perform sacrifices with all mantras.
Thus ends the fourth chapter of the Śrī Kramadīpikā.
Having performed this rite in the month of Caitra during the bright fortnight under an auspicious asterism, and having received initiation from the preceptor, one—
authorized by him— should commence the preliminary service (*pūrvassevā*) on the twelfth day of the pure [fortnight] in the second month.
Having performed the rites beginning with bathing and ending with the worship of the body, following the path previously described, the preeminent practitioner—
pure, observing silence, celibate, eating at night, and with a tranquil soul through recitation— [should use] a rosary of white lotus seeds.
Offering service to his body, giving mouthfuls of fodder to the cows, extending compassion toward all living beings,
and saluting Durgā— the presiding deity of the mantra and the sun that dispels the darkness difficult to penetrate.
And the teacher.
Performing his own duties while remaining within the system of castes and stages of life, he should consecrate himself with mantras at the time of bathing;
when eating food, he should consume it after reciting the *ācamana* formula seven times, multiplied by the number of the principles (*tattva*).
Water and so forth.
One should recite the excellent ten-syllable mantra four times ten thousand times, separately and in sequence;
if it is the eighteen-syllable mantra, the prescribed number is said to be twenty thousand.

Vegetables, roots, fruits, curds produced from cow’s udders, alms-food, grain, flour, and milk-rice—by giving these in sequence at different locations such as mountain peaks and so forth, one becomes a giver of food.
When one is unable to provide all of these, I have here described this preliminary rite of service (*pūrvassevā*) to be performed. Once this is completed, [the main practice follows].
Furthermore, for the sake of accomplishment, the lord of practitioners should recite [the mantra] again according to the rule.
At the conclusion of the bodily worship, at the beginning of the daily purification, and having resorted to either the procedure taught for initiation or another [authorized] injunction,
one should worship Kṛṣṇa in a secluded house, seated there, consuming the remnants of the oblation.
Having recited ten hundred thousand times the ten-syllable mantra which bestows inexhaustible fruit,
one of pure intellect should offer ten thousand oblations into the fire with fresh, reddish lotuses drenched in jaggery, clarified butter, and honey.
If the mantra consists of a pair of vowels, one should recite it five hundred thousand times and perform oblations as prescribed for half a hundred thousand.
If pure materials are unavailable, one should begin the rite of homa with lotus flowers mixed with ghee and sugar.
Others say that for the twice-born, the king, and the Vaiśya who are unable to perform the fire-oblation (homa), the recitation (japa) should be performed multiplied by eight hundred;
however, if it is with the homa, their japa here is equal [to the number of oblations]. That which was prescribed for the castes when devoid of homa is indeed [the same].
This was ordained for those of tremulous glances.

Whatever caste a Śūdra may belong to, he should perform the prescribed recitation (japa) for those women with curved brows, being faithful to the ritual injunctions and with his body bowed in devotion.
Having been consecrated again by the preceptor according to the ritual rules and having bestowed a sacrificial fee upon him, he should,
filled with devotion, gratify the Brahmins with abundant offerings of food and wealth.

Having thus accomplished either one of these two excellent mantras through recitation and other means, the wise devotee whose mind is fixed on Acyuta should daily worship Mukunda according to the prescribed rite during the three sessions of the day.
Then, within a pavilion shimmering with gems set in a golden ground, situated in a magnificent garden—
Seated upon a meditation throne at the center of a radiant jeweled ground beneath a blossoming *kalpa* tree;

possessing the deep blue luster of a great sapphire, with exceedingly long hair that falls in glossy, dark curls over his forehead; his face as charming as a full-blown lotus surrounded by swarms of bees, and his eyes like glorious blue water-lilies.
With cheeks blooming and radiant with swinging earrings, a beautiful nose, and lips as red as the finest vermilion, his face was graced by a gentle smile;
he wore upon his neck a shimmering ornament of many gems, and he bore the *pauṇḍarīka* mark on his nails.
His chest was anointed with the dust raised from cows, his limbs were well-nourished, and he blazed with the splendor of ornaments made of gold.
Upon the region of his hips and the pair of his beautiful calves, he is bound with a girdle of tinkling clusters of small bells;
he laughs with the magnificent luster of his lotus-like hands and feet, which possess the radiance of blooming bandhūjīva flowers;
in his right hand he holds milk-rice (*pāyasa*), and in his left hand he holds fresh, pure *haiyaṅgavīna* butter.

Having recollected Viṣṇu—who has crushed the hosts of enemies of the gods who constitute a burden to the earth; who is intent on slaying Pūtanā and others; who is surrounded by a multitude of cowherd women, cowherds, and cattle; and who is worshipped by the lords of the gods and the hosts of deities—one should worship Him at dawn with devotion, bowing low, using the limbs of His body and the thunderbolt and other weapons as offerings.
One should satisfy Him with white rice, fresh butter (*haiyaṅgavīna*), and milk mixed with curd. Thus, the man who, endowed with constant faith, worships Acyuta every day at dawn,
shall before long obtain complete prosperity in this world and, after death, the pure supreme abode.
May it be so! Having worshipped Śauri every day at the beginning of the day, one should offer [the oblation] with curd or with water mixed with jaggery.
Having offered libations into the mouth of the Illustrious One, one should then recite that mantra one thousand and eight times with devotion;
this is the distinguished form of the midday recitation ritual, which is to be honored by the foremost gods, sages, and celestial beings.
Surrounded by throngs of cows, cowherds, and cowherd women; with limbs that were beautiful and well-formed, possessing a dense luster like the rising sun;
with lovely braided hair adorned with ear-ornaments fashioned from peacock feathers; and with eyes as large as lotuses and sparkling side-locks of hair.
His face is like the orb of the full moon; his cheeks possess the splendor of jeweled earrings; he has a beautiful nose and a most lovely, gentle smile.
He wears yellow garments, and his limbs are radiant with brilliant anklets, necklaces, waist-bands, armlets, bracelets, and other ornaments.
His body is tinged with divine unguents, he wears a radiant and unfading variegated forest garland, and he is inflamed by the god of love;
he is blowing a flute or holding it in his own hand, while in his left hand he holds a small drum and a staff for tending cattle—
his noble flute resounds.

Having meditated upon the bull-bannered Lord (Śiva) holding an excellent jewel in his right hand, which is skillful in granting desired boons, one should worship the Son of Nanda for the attainment of prosperity;

and having worshipped Him according to the prescribed rite with offerings such as garlands, and by honoring His limbs, His beloved consort, and the feet of His friends with Indra-vajra and other mantras.
Having offered the sacrificial food (nivedya) prepared according to the prescribed rules for initiation, one should duly present it in an excellent golden vessel.
Then, one should perform one hundred and eight oblations with milk-rice mixed with ghee and well-refined sugar.

With a generous heart, one should offer oblations (*bali*) in one's own directions to the hosts of gods, sages, yogis, and attendant deities. At the conclusion of the worship, with the thought that it is clarified butter mixed with milk-rice (*pāyasa*), the practitioner, having sprinkled water upon its mouth, should recite the mantra one thousand and eight or even one hundred times.
That foremost of men who daily worships with devotion that Beloved of the Cowherdesses in the midst of the day—
him all the gods shall eternally revere, and indeed all the worlds shall remain under his control.
He shall be endowed with intelligence, longevity, prosperity, beauty, and good fortune, along with sons, friends, cattle, land, jewels, and grain.
May he be further enriched by abundant other enjoyments, and may that abode known as Acyuta be attained again and again.
Regarding the third period of worship, there is no distinction of time.
Regarding the time—whether at evening or at night—some wise ones say:
if [the mantra] consists of ten syllables, it should be performed at night; if it consists of eighteen syllables, it should be performed at evening;
others have declared that one should perform both [types of rites] by means of both [times].
In the evening, at Dvāravatī,
which was adorned with wonderful gardens and beautified by sixteen thousand palaces,
[there were lakes] crowded with swans and cranes and graced with lotuses and water-lilies.
In that most excellent palace, surrounded by lakes of pure water,
within a jeweled pavilion whose splendor equaled the radiance of the rising sun,
Hari sat upon a golden lotus-throne with a soft cushion.
Surrounded by Nārada and others during the definitive exposition of the reality of the Self,
he was bestowing his own abode— the supreme, imperishable state— upon those sages;
he was as dark as a blue lotus, gentle, and possessed of eyes as broad as lotus petals.
Resplendent with a crown and diadem adorned by glossy earrings,
with a beautiful and serene countenance and shimmering shark-shaped earrings;
with the Śrīvatsa mark upon his chest, shining with the Kaustubha gem, and wearing a garland of forest flowers.
His chest was anointed with saffron from Kashmir, he wore garments of yellow silk,
and was adorned with necklaces, armlets, bracelets, anklets, and other ornaments;
having taken upon himself the vast burden of the entire earth, his mind was filled with joy.

Having thus meditated upon [the deity] with four resplendent arms holding a conch, a discus, a mace, and a lotus, the practitioner of mantra should worship; this constitutes the first enclosure with the limbs (aṅgas).
The second [enclosure] is performed with the queens, and one should worship the third [enclosure].
Nārada, Parvata, Jiṣṇu, Niśaṭha, Uddhava, Dāruka, Viśvaksena, Śaileya, and the son of Vinatā (Garuḍa) were stationed at the front in the various directions;
then there was a second enclosure consisting of the world-protectors and their respective weapons.
Having thus worshipped according to the prescribed rite, one should offer milk-rice (*pāyasa*).
Having gratified Hari with water mixed with sugar-candy, imagining it to be milk,
the practitioner of mantra (*mantrī*) should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times while meditating upon Puruṣottama.
One should perform the fire-oblation (homa) during all worship ceremonies, or at midday.

Having performed the rites from the seat (āsana) up to the water-offering (arghya), the wise one should offer praise and bow down. Then, having offered oneself and performed the ritual dismissal (udvāsya), one should place the deity within the lotus of one's own heart.
Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) and become one with that [deity], one should worship oneself again.
That man who thus constantly worships Vāsudeva in the evening shall attain all desires and, at the end, go to the supreme goal.
If at night one should worship the son of Devakī, whose mind is overcome by passion,
who is weary from the *rāsa* dance and stands in the midst of the circle of cowherd girls—
one should drive a peg into the ground that is broad, well-rounded, smooth, and one *vitasti* in height.

Trampling one another with their feet and embracing with their hands— this indeed is the circular dance of the *rāsa* assembly. It takes place upon a vast, white sandbank, cooled by a breeze laden with the pollen from the roots of land-lotuses and filled with a multitude of spray-drops from the waves.

In that place, which was agitated by hundreds of millions of women mangled by sharp, bodiless arrows, and where swarms of female bees roamed through the expanse of water made clear by the rays of the moon;
By Vidyādharas, Kinnaras, Siddhas, and Suras, along with Gandharvas, Bhujaṅgamas, and Cāraṇas—
mounted upon their excellent celestial chariots, stationed in the sky, and showering heaps of flowers—
the arrangement of dwellings and pastimes was fashioned for the throngs of joyful women who were joined together in pairs.
He who had assumed his own divine form in many ways even while within the body of Maṇiśaṅku;

who was perceived separately by the two beautiful-eyed women as being inside each of them; whose pair of arms were entwined around their beloveds like a nest of vines; and who was joined with horripilation that quivered from the agitation caused by the fire of Love (Anaṅga) blazing forth through their union with him.

With the seven musical notes, which are most pleasing as they are differentiated by various scales, and with the rhythms and clusters of beats; with the beautiful resonance of the clearly visible circles of noble jewels whirling upon the life-breaths;
