thus, the body is divided by gems, yet joined together by emeralds and gold.
Seated in the center of a vast, ruddy lotus, its stalk fashioned from jewels;
his body possessing the luster of an *atasī* flower, yet not reddish, with eyes like the petals of a young, crimson lotus;
his mass of hair bound by a peacock’s tail-feathers, shimmering with clusters of beautiful blossoms upon fresh sprouts.
Her face was like the full moon and other moons; her pair of cheeks was adorned with jeweled earrings;
her lip was like the face of a rabbit [the moon]; she wore various kinds of ornaments made of the finest gems;
her radiant face was covered by a garment bright as a flower-blossom; she was the very ground of exquisite grace and charm.
I meditate upon the sole preceptor of the universe, whose soles are as auspicious as fresh coral, whose arms shine with garlands swarming with bees,
whose chest is reddened by the saffron from the embrace of a young woman’s breasts,
who moves with a graceful gait, who is intent on singing songs inspired by Śiva’s flute, and who is pierced by the arrows of Cupid.
One should worship, according to the rules, the Formless and the Born (Aja) within the most excellent seat first mentioned;
having first worshipped that, one should then worship the enclosure of its limbs and the couples residing in the flavors.
Then, upon the sixteen petals, one should worship the group of vowels and the Mūrtis together with their Śaktis, situated in the supreme rasa.

Having thus properly worshipped Hari— who is accompanied by Saramā and his own arts, who is the half of the divine couple, and who is surrounded by Indra and others in fourfold circles— the one of tender mind,
having offered well-cooked milk-rice with sugar into a silver or golden cup, should present it.
If one possesses the means, one should offer milk with sugar, individually in sixteen bronze cups, to each of the couples in succession; then, as before, one should perform the entire rite.
He who, with a noble heart, regularly performs this ritual that deludes the entire world at night after night—
Indeed, he who has attained the glorious and immovable state becomes worthy of worship by all the world and goes to the infinite.
One should always worship Acyuta with devotion at night or at the end of the day;
for both yield equal fruit for one who desires to cross over this cycle of existence.
Thus, for one who worships the Enemy of Madhu (Viṣṇu) during the night with such a mental form,

in the hand of that very Lord— who is beloved by all classes of living beings and whose abode is the daughter of the ocean— stand the trees of Dharma, Artha, Kāma, and Mokṣa, as prayed for by the virtuous group.
The rows of whose fruits drip with the liquid essence of the nectar of intense bliss.

Now it is said: at the conclusion of the worship of the Supreme Person as previously described, there is indeed an alternative ritual procedure for the libations even in rites performed for specific desires; for the fruit shall certainly be attained even without the formal worship. Having first satisfied the Śaktis one by one with the recitation-mantras, one should then satisfy Acyuta therein.
Having invoked [the deity] and worshipped with all waters and offerings,
and having then formed the *dhenumudrā* (cow-seal), one should prepare the materials for libation (*tarpaṇa*) with water; then,
with the thought that it is [the deity], one should offer libations with that water held in an *añjali* joined like a golden goblet.
The number twenty-eight is prescribed for the libations offered during the three periods of the day.
One should offer libations once each to the retinues assigned to their respective times.
At dawn, one should offer curd mixed with jaggery; at midday, milk-rice with fresh butter.
"Milk with sugar-candy at the third period" is the substance thus declared.
The word "I satisfy" (tarpayāmi) should be joined to these names at the end of the mantras.
However, when [the names] end in the accusative case, one should complete the remainder of the worship.
Having sprinkled himself with those same waters of grace, he should drink the water;
having recited that [mantra] and then dismissed it, being absorbed in that [deity], he should recite the mantra.
Now, the materials for the optional rites will be described;
in those propitiatory offerings, one should worship by resorting to any one of the prescribed methods.
One should satisfy this [deity] with sixteen materials, either once or four times.

With devotion, one should offer to Acyuta milk-rice, curd-rice, rice-and-pulse, wheat-flour balls in molasses, milk, curd, fresh butter, clarified butter, plantain, banana-fruit, lotus-pollen, fragrant sweets, and cakes— each preceded and followed by water, and repeated four times with milk and other offerings.
Flattened rice (pṛthuka) combined with parched grain (lāja)— these sixteen substances are prescribed here. Having offered a heap of white sugar before the final milk at the end of the parched grains,
the man who daily gratifies Hari in this manner forty-seven times every morning [attains his goal].

For one whose mind is focused on no other, all desired perfections are held in the palm of his hand through this mandala. One should satisfy [the deity] twelve times with these nine offerings: milk still warm from the udder, boiled milk, curd, fresh butter, ghee, rice cooked in milk, sugar-candy, honey, and nectar.
This is another procedure for libation (*tarpaṇa*), which yields results equal to those previously described when performed eight hundred times;
it is specifically prescribed for magical rites (*kārmaṇa-karman*), for fame, and especially for gathering people together.
Having offered libations while proceeding through a city or even a village with the thought that Mukunda is present in every drop of warm water, [one attains the desired result].
The minister shall obtain delicious food for his own servants, as well as garments, grains, and wealth;
for as many times as the minister satisfies [the deity] with libations, for that same number of times he should worship the mantra.
By means of this very libation alone, he shall accomplish all his undertakings.
That twice-born one who here subsists on alms— Nanda’s son himself— who wanders about begging for alms while sporting with the beautiful-eyed cowherd girls,
enriching [the offering] with curds and milk through his own most charming and playful jests; [by him, the world is filled].
He obtains an abundance of alms.

One should draw the fire-city casket (analapura-puṭa) with six corners in the middle; in its pericarp, one should write Kandarpa joined with the person to be accomplished (sādhya), and the six syllables located in the gaps [of the corners] twice upon the filaments.

In the center of the ten syllables— preceded by *Śakti* and *Śrī*, and followed by the two syllables *Kali* and the nine-syllable mantra— one should place the lotus of each of the ten letters of the king of mantras.
This should be written with a golden needle using yellow pigment (*gorocanā*), encircled by the abode of the earth, and adorned with the god of love bearing a blood-red garland.
This *gopālayantṛ* (cowherd-protector), fashioned as a pill upon a cloth made of gold, is said to bestow all desired objects;
when sprinkled with the *sampāta* [remnants of offerings] and consecrated by the great ones, it is capable of subjugating the world through the power of its refuge.
Those desiring protection, fame, sons, land, wealth, grain, prosperity, and good fortune should constantly [use] this [remedy] of unsurpassed potency for those afflicted by possession by spirits,
insanity, epilepsy, poison, fainting, and irregular fevers.
Meditating on the head, one should mutter this mantra to instantly pacify all disturbances:
"The Lord who traversed the three worlds, the wielder of the discus, whose heart is of black iron.
This six-syllabled mantra is proclaimed as the bestower of all accomplishments.
The chest is illuminated by fire; the illusory one has a head marked with a *lavala* flower.
This very power is supreme, subtle, eternal consciousness, whose nature is self-awareness.
The seed-syllable of Lakṣmī is said to consist of the letters *asthi*, *agni*, *govinda*, and *lava*. From these two [groups], there arises an eighteen-lettered mantra;
with these, one may worship in a Śālagrāma stone, a mantra, a yantra, a maṇḍala, or in images.
"Daily worship of Tare should be performed, and not merely upon the ground. Thus,
he who here constantly worships Mukunda by means of recitation, oblations, worship, libations, and so forth, relying solely on one of the two mantras;
But he, having attained all enjoyments through long and arduous effort, returns once more to that most excellent abode of Viṣṇu.
Thus ends the fifth chapter of the Kramadīpikā.
Now I shall describe the applications of both mantras equally,
as well as certain other mantras of infinite power that accomplish their respective purposes.
I bow to that son of Devakī, who is newly born, possessing radiant luster,

clad in yellow garments, and holding in his hands the discus, conch, mace, and lotus. Having meditated thus, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times for the purpose of crossing over the ocean of worldly existence.
One who, being well-composed, offers ten thousand oblations of sweet and abundant *pālāśa* flowers with either of the two mantras,
shall obtain memory, intelligence, fortitude, and strength, and become a preeminent poet.
One might think that another [mantra] would yield the same fruit as recitation, meditation, and fire-offerings;
therefore, one should always take refuge in the glorious feet of Mukunda by uttering: "I seek refuge" (*ahaṃ prapadye*). This is the eighteen-syllable mantra of Mukunda.
The Gāyatrī of Nārada, preceded by the Ṛṣis beginning with Mudgala—
whosoever drinks water every morning after reciting it one hundred and eight times,
that man shall, within six months, become a possessor of the Veda (Śrutidhara).

One should recite the mantra while meditating upon the Child, whose divine limbs are fully formed, resting as before on his mother’s lap, with moving hands and feet, and possessing a dark-blue luster;
one should likewise offer ten thousand oblations of clarified butter into the sacrificial fire.
At the end of this entire [mantra], with the sound vibrating like the wind, one should offer devotion that is as unsteady as a flickering moth, along with faith and eternal peace,
using either this [mantra] or the following: "To the one whose nature is the play of a child, hūṃ phaṭ namaḥ."
The *gāyatrī* of Nalakūvara is called "Bālakṛṣṇa.
Through its recitation and other rites, all perfections (*siddhi*)—beginning with those of the seers (*ṛṣi*)—shall be attained here and hereafter.
When the infant was placed upon his cradle and began to cry, he was [comforted] by the cowherd women.
Beholding [the deity] with the thought that it is milk, one should satisfy [it]; thus he partakes of food.
At the end of the form of the child (bāla-rūpa), one should utter the word "rasa-rūpa" (having the nature of essence).
[The mantra is: "Obeisance to the pair of forms of satisfaction and obeisance, to the Lord of the subsequent [deities]."

"Offer food with the mantra 'svāhā'"; this thirty-syllable mantra for the giver of food has Nārada as its seer, the Anuṣṭubh as its meter, and the lords of food as its presiding deities, beginning with the Ṛṣis.
It protects against afflictions such as possession by spirits, children's diseases, planetary influences, insanity, and loss of memory.

One should recite the mantra while remembering the child as one who has drunk from the breast of Pūtanā and whose head was seized; and while visualizing her weeping, with all her limbs pierced by the *sāsucuṣaṇa* [demon],
all the seizing spirits (*grahas*), having entered him, will release him and flee swiftly.
One should offer oblations of *kharamañjarī* blossoms into the fire;

having bathed with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), one should cause [the disciple] to consume the remaining *gavya* in the presence of Pūtanā and the Lord of the Face, and consecrate him with that water from the ritual jar.
This should be accomplished by reciting it one thousand times for the pacification of all calamities, using this twelve-syllable mantra:
*hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*, or with the word *astika* appended.
Its seer and other attributes are those of the Brahma-Gāyatrī; it destroys the influence of the planets and removes diseases.
One should recite one of the two mantras ten thousand times while contemplating the cart overturned by one’s own lotus feet,
for the pacification of all obstacles.
The ancillary rites (aṅgas) for these mantras consist of worship with the wheels and other components.
May Hari protect you— he who is always proclaimed as the source of prosperity through his limbs, which are like those of Indra and others, and his vajra and other weapons;
he whose body is blue like a young child, who holds curd and honeyed milk-rice with his two arms,
and who is adorned with a network of tinkling bells made of tigers’ claws.
Having meditated thus, one should offer oblations into the fire with three hundred sprouts of *śatavīryā*,
soaked in milk and clarified butter, while reciting the mantra one hundred thousand times.
Then, having given the sacrificial fee to the preceptor, one should feed the most eminent of the twice-born.

He shall live for a hundred years free from disease; of this there is no doubt. Furthermore, at the end of the twelve syllables, one should address Puruṣottama with another mantra, saying to the powerful Viṣṇu: "Grant me long life."
I pay homage; this mantra consists of thirty-two syllables, its seer is Nārada, its meter is Anuṣṭubh, and its deity is Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Now I shall state its limbs: [the syllables] joined with the sun (12), the elements (5), the senses (5), the Vasus (8), the eyes (2), and the breaths (5) for the Self.
Having recited this mantra one hundred thousand times through the stages of Mahānada, Pratijyotis, Māyā, and Vidyā, and having offered ten thousand oblations of milk-rice (pāyasa),
and then offering oblations of dūrvā grass as before, one shall obtain an exceedingly long life.
Having grasped Kṛṣṇa by his two beaks as he was tearing at Baka with his two arms,
one should remember [the Lord] during the distress of children; by touching one of them and practicing this mantra,
and by anointing them with sesame seeds over which it has been recited, they shall become happy.
Here too, another Manu, the beloved of Fire, spoke of Him who, in the form of a young boy,
was tending cattle while sounding His flute during the protection of the cows; and he likewise spoke of the state of a cowherd for Him who had assumed the guise of a householder.
For Vāsudeva, the mantra consists of eighteen syllables: *vāsudevāya varma-astra-śikhā-syāḥ*.

The sage is Nārada, the meter is Gāyatrī, and the deity is Kṛṣṇa; or alternatively, one may perform the protection of the cowherds with this mantra, employing the discus and other weapons as the limbs (*aṅga*) of the rite. A wise person should perform it in this manner.

When suffering from the pain of being bitten by a *kumbhīnasa* or other such snakes, the wise man should remember Hari dancing upon the hoods of the serpent Kālīya; he should practice [this visualization] on whichever part of his body was bitten,
imagining that the Lord is sprinkling that very body with a glance that rains down nectar.
Threatening him with his left index finger, he quickly releases [the victim] from poison;
having filled a water-pot with water while recollecting the subduer of Kālīya,
and having chanted [the mantra] one hundred and eight times, he should sprinkle it upon the poisoned person, and that person shall become well.
Having uttered two-syllable [mantras] within the middle of the *kāvyam*, at the end, and within the hood [of the serpent],
one should always speak again immediately thereafter;
having said "I bow to the Son of Devakī," [one proceeds] by means of the sound of dancing.
"Manu Daṇḍalipi says one should address King Acyuta thus:
the sage of this [mantra] is the seer Nārada; its limbs are formed by the feet taken both individually and collectively;
the meter is Anuṣṭubh; and the deity is Kṛṣṇa, the subduer of Kālīya."
One should recite the excellent mantra one hundred thousand times and offer oblations with clarified butter.
Its worship is prescribed with the limbs [of the mantra], the guardians of the directions, Vajra, and so forth;
or else, all the rites previously mentioned should be performed by means of this very [mantra].
Indeed, there is no mantra in this world equal to this for neutralizing poison.
By him, pills were prepared from the ground pulp of the *śukataru* tree with cow’s urine; these are destroyers of venom when administered through drinking, nasal drops, collyrium, or ointment.
Meditating upon Hari— who holds Mount Govardhana with his left arm raised like a staff,
and whose face is fixed upon a flute held between the fingers of his other hand—
one should recite one of the two mantras while walking without an umbrella.
For him, there shall never be fear from rain, wind, or lightning; indeed,
by meditating upon the one who has caused Indra to abandon his efforts against the mass of futile clouds,
he shall undoubtedly be free from the calamity of drought for a period of twelve years.
He was sporting in the middle of the Yamunā through activities such as diving and splashing about,
while being sprinkled by his beloved women with showers of water droplets from her spray.
Having meditated thus, one should offer ten thousand oblations with water-sprinkled *vānīra* twigs;
even in an unseasonable time, a great rain will fall—of this there is no doubt.
By remembering [the deity] at the very beginning upon one's head, [one is freed] from poison, boils, fever, and the like.
For one afflicted by the delusions of the six states of existence, recitation [of this mantra] brings peace in an instant.
Alternatively, one may meditate upon Acyuta (Viṣṇu), mounted upon Garuḍa, accompanied by Bala and Pradyumna,
and intent on crushing the fever of one's own afflictions with his own fever.
Having meditated thus, one should apply [the mantra] to the head of one overcome by fever;
even an incurable fever accompanied by complications will attain peace in an instant.
Having meditated and worshipped [the deity] immersed [in water], [one should offer oblations] with four-finger-width pieces of wood soaked in milk.
One should offer ten thousand oblations with pieces of the *amṛta* plant for the pacification of fever.
Having remembered Hari, who removes the terrifying heat [of affliction] like a sharp autumnal arrow piercing its mark,
one should touch the afflicted person with both hands and recite the mantra for the pacification of disease.
For the destruction of untimely death, one should meditate upon Him who restored the son of Sāndīpani and offer ten thousand oblations of pieces of the nectar-creeper smeared with milk;
[He who] was giving a son along with Arjuna to the Brahmin whose son had died.
Having meditated, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times for the increase of one’s sons.
One should offer ten thousand oblations into the fire using *putrajīva* wood as fuel;
by offering its fruits smeared with honey, his sons and others shall become long-lived.
Having worshipped a water-pot filled with a decoction of milk-tree (kṣīradru) at night and having recited [the mantra] ten thousand times,
one should sprinkle a woman in the morning for twelve days;
even if she is barren, she will give birth to sons who are long-lived and free from disease.
There is no doubt that she attains this; for a woman who eats ghee while reciting [the mantra],
if she recites it one hundred and eight times in the morning and drinks water from the folded leaves of the *vodhicchada* tree for one month, she will obtain a son.
O son of Devakī, O Govinda, O Vāsudeva, O Lord of the Universe! Grant me a son, O God; I have come to you for refuge. Having defeated the *kṛtyā* sent by my enemy, the King of Kāśī.
Meditating on Hari as he burns that city with his splendor,
one should offer oblations of mustard seeds smeared with oil at night for seven days;
thus enraged, he will destroy the very author of the magical spell (kṛtyā).
Having meditated upon Acyuta seated in a divine hermitage adorned with groves of *badarī* trees,
touching the body of Ghaṇṭākarṇa with his two lotus-like hands,
one should offer a hundred thousand oblations of sesame seeds soaked in the three sweets (*trimadhu*).

Or one should mutter [the mantra] for the pacification of all sins and for the beauty of the body; while remembering Hari, one should cause Rukmi and Bala—who were intent on hatred and powerless at dice—to be defeated. For the sake of desired offerings, one should sacrifice pills made from cow dung.
Having meditated upon Acyuta— seated upon Garuḍa, raining down arrows resembling blazing fire,
and pursuing the host of Brahmins as they flee—
one should practice one mantra seven thousand times.
This shall effect the eradication of enemies within seven days.
Meditating on [the deity] as one who has uprooted a calf and is carrying a *kapiṇya* fruit, one should recite the mantra ten thousand times; he causes the target to be eradicated at that very moment.
Having meditated upon himself as the slayer of Kaṃsa, fallen upon the ground,
and having dragged out the lifeless soul of Kaṃsa, one should recite the mantra ten thousand times;
and one should offer oblations for him with ten thousand libations of clarified butter.
Even an enemy who has consumed nectar will undoubtedly die;
or else, one should offer oblations of fuel-sticks from the *akṣa* tree smeared with neem oil.
By reciting the mantra ten thousand times at night, the enemy is slain in an instant.

Standing in a cremation ground at night, one should perform a fire sacrifice for the pacification of enemies, offering the leaves of the *doṣāriṣṭa* tree, the three pungent spices (*vyoṣa*), cotton seeds, and snake-hoods, all smeared with castor oil.
Killing rites are not recommended; however, if one must perform such a rite, one should recite the mantra ten thousand times.
Or, with a tranquil mind, one desiring peace should offer oblations of milk-rice (pāyasa) for that long;

or, desiring victory, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times while remembering Hari, the remover of the *pārijāta* tree. For such a person, defeat shall never arise from any source whatsoever.

Meditating upon Hari seated on his chariot, bestowing the meaning of the Gītā upon Pārtha and with hands in the gesture of exposition (vyākhyāmudrā), one should mutter [the mantra] for the increase of dharma and for tranquility:
one hundred thousand times with *pālāśa* flowers, or ten thousand times with those soaked in honey.
One who explains all the scriptures shall become a skilled poet and a king of debaters.
[He beholds] Hari, who assumes the universal form, whose radiant splendor is equal to ten million rising suns,
who resembles molten gold, and whose nature consists of both fire and moon.
[One should meditate upon] the lotus-feet of [the Lord], whose mouth is as radiant as the sun and fire, adorned with divine ornaments, bearing various weapons,
and pervading the entire expanse of the universe;
[these feet are to be invoked] for the protection of the kingdom, the city, the village, the dwelling, and the body.
One should recite one of the two mantras with devotion while meditating upon it;

or else, [one may recite the mantra] which has Arjuna as its seer (*ṛṣi*), the *triṣṭubh* as its meter (*chandas*), and Viṣṇu in his universal form (*viśvarūpa*) as its presiding deity (*adhidaivata*), with all the limbs [of the body] arranged separately.
One should recite the Gītā-mantra in a place such as that of Aṣīkeśa with the utterances of "Om" and so forth;
or, for the sake of total protection and the pacification of all obstacles, one should perform oblations (homa).

Thus ends the sixth chapter of the Kramadīpikā. I shall now describe the practice for the attainment of inexhaustible wealth, which is kept strictly secret by the fortunate ones, such as Dhananātha and others, and is performed by them constantly.
In Dvāravatī, which was surrounded by excellent palaces as radiant as a thousand suns,
by numerous wish-fulfilling trees, and adorned with jewels;
where the pillars, doors, arches, and walls were composed of blazing gems.

In the midst of a jeweled river and a ground of rubies, beneath a celestial tree that incessantly pours forth streams of water-jewels, where variegated canopies adorned with blooming garlands hang down with dangling pearls.
Seated upon a lotus lion-throne of jewels resembling the rising sun, amidst the quarters of the sky illuminated by rows of jewel-lamps,
the infallible Acyuta— resembling molten gold— is the object of meditation.
Possessing a splendor equal to ten million rising moons, suns, and lightning flashes;
beautiful in every limb, gentle, and adorned with all ornaments;
clad in yellow garments, his arms shining with the discus, conch, mace, and lotus.
Touching with the tip of his left lotus-foot the water-pot— which has the luster of a fresh sprout and from which a continuous stream of jewels is incessantly gushing forth—
he [showered] Rukmiṇī and Satyabhāmā upon their heads with a flow of masses of gems.
Nāgnajitī and Sunandā, standing on the right and left [of the central pair], pour from the water-pots held in their right and left hands, bestowing those two pots upon them;
and Mitravindā and Sulakṣaṇā, standing on the right and left of those two, likewise do so.
Having drawn forth two jars filled with jewels from the two rivers of jewels,
Jāmbavatī and Sūśīlā stand at his right and left hands respectively;
outside, his sixteen thousand beloved wives are arranged all around him.
They should be meditated upon as radiant with water-pots (kalaśas) joined by streams of gold and heaps of jewels;
outside of them are the eight treasures (nidhis), filling the earth with wealth;
and outside of those are all the Vṛṣṇis, as well as the gods and others, as previously described.
Having thus meditated upon the Supreme Self, one should mutter the twenty-syllable mantra four hundred thousand times;
one should offer oblations of clarified butter forty thousand times.
The eighteen-syllable and twenty-syllable mantras are preceded by the words *śakti* and *śrī*.
There is indeed no other mantra equal to this one in the three worlds.
Brahmā is its seer (*ṛṣi*), the Gāyatrī is its meter (*chandaḥ*), and Kṛṣṇa is its deity (*devatā*).
The conceptualization of its seed-syllable (*bīja*), power (*śakti*), and so forth, is exactly as previously stated.
13) Now the ritual procedure (*kalpa*) for this mantra, as spoken by Sanatkumāra, is being declared.
Having performed the deposition upon the seats (*pīṭhanyāsa*) up to its conclusion according to the previously stated sequence, the wise practitioner [should proceed].
One should place the six limbs upon the surfaces of the ten fingers of both hands;

having performed the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka*) with the mantra, one should place the *mātṛkā* encapsulated by the *manu* (seed-syllable) and the ten principles (*tattvas*) according to the sequence of withdrawal and emanation.
Furthermore, having performed the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka*), one should assign the syllables of the mantra to the body:
on the head, the forehead, between the eyebrows, the two eyes, the ears, the nostrils,
the mouth, the chin, the throat, the base of the arms, the heart, and the navel.

One should perform the placement (nyāsa) at the navel, the genitals, the base (ādhāra), the hips, the knees, the shanks, the ankles, and the feet; this is declared to be the process of emanation (sṛṣṭi). The process of maintenance (sthiti) extends from the heart to the feet, while the process of withdrawal (saṃhṛti) begins from the feet.

Having thus established the cage of the five forms five times in their order of persistence and dissolution, and having performed the rites of emanation and maintenance, one should perform the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) using the syllables of the mantra [corresponding to] the qualities, fires, Vedas, organs, instruments, and senses.
Having formed the mudrās, one should perform the binding of the directions (digbandha) as before, starting with the crown (kirīṭa).
Having meditated and recited [the mantra], one should worship the body according to the "cage of forms" (mūrttipañjara) and other rites.
Alternatively, one should worship Viṣṇu externally; for that purpose, the yantra is described.
Having smeared the ground with cow dung, one should place a pedestal there.
Having smeared it with fragrant paste, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus.
Within the pericarp, one should draw a hexagon; there, one should place the God of Love (Manmatha) together with the object of the rite (sādhya).
One should then encircle Smara with the remaining seventeen syllables.
In the corners of the east, the southeast, and the northwest, one should place Śrī, and in the remaining corners, Saṃvit.

One should write the six-syllable *smaragāyatrī* at the joints and on the filaments, three times each; the *mālāmantra* on the eight petals, six times each; and having written it thus, one should encircle the exterior with the letters of the *mātṛkā*.
One should draw the image of the earth on the outside, [surrounded] by the Śrī-māyā in the cardinal and intermediate directions.
Having inscribed this yantra on plates of gold or other materials as previously described,
whoever wears it— once consecrated— is honored even by the gods.

The Gāyatrī mantra for Kāmadeva consists of the two words "kāmadeva" and "puṣpavāṇa," each ending in the dative case (ṅe). It is joined with "vidmahe" and "dhīmahi," followed by "tanno'naṅgaḥ pracodayāt.
This mantra, which delights the people, is to be recited at the beginning of the chanting of the Gopāla mantras.

At the end of the *natya*, having uttered "to Kāmadeva" with the dative case-ending (*ṅe*), followed by "beloved of all people" (*sarvajanapriyam*); then, after "all people" (*sarvajana*), likewise the word "deluder" (*sammohana*);
and having uttered "blaze, blaze, blaze intensely" (*jvala jvala projjvala*) for "of all people" (*sarvajanasya*).
"O Śiva, speak the heart-mantra for me: 'Vaśaṃ kuru yugam.
This Madana-mantra, consisting of forty-eight syllables and enriched with the essential seed-syllable, brings the three worlds under one's control when used at the beginning of recitation."
The underground chamber should be square and adorned with eight spikes (or vajras).
Having worshipped the pedestal as before and conceived the anthropomorphic form (puruṣamūrti),
one should invoke Acyuta there with devotion, perform the ritual of the limbs (sakalīkaraṇa), and worship Him.
One should then worship Him again according to the sequence of ritual placement (nyāsa), beginning from the seat (āsana) up to the ornaments (vibhūṣā).

Having worshipped, as before, with scents, unbroken rice, and flowers using the root mantra, the crown, the two earrings, the six limbs of creation and maintenance, the conch, discus, mace, lotus, garland, the *śrīvatsa* mark, and the *kaustubha* gem;
First, one should worship the limbs in the corners of the two fire-palaces (triangles), in sequence as follows:
the Heart, the Head, the Crest, the Armor, the Eye, and the Weapon.
Then [one worships] Vāsudeva, Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha.
At the bases of the petals starting from the southeast (Agni), Śānti, Śrī, Sarasvatī,
and Rati are to be worshipped; then one should worship the eight queens in the cardinal petals,
beginning with Rukmiṇī and the others, proceeding from right to left at the tips of the petals.
Then, one should worship sixteen thousand beloved ones all at once;
one should worship in sequence the eight treasures (nidhis), beginning with Indranīla and Mukunda, as well as Makara, Ānanda, Kacchapa, Śaṅkha, Padma, and the others.
Outside of that, one should worship the enclosures beginning with Indra and Vajra.
Having thus worshipped Acyuta, who is surrounded by these seven enclosures, with devotion,
one should gratify him with milk-rice mixed with curds, sugar-candy, and clarified butter.
Having offered the royal services, praised and bowed to Keśava,

one should dissolve Him into one's own heart along with the host of attendants. Having established oneself [in that state] and worshipped thoroughly, being absorbed in Him, one should mutter the mantra.
In the Ratnābhiṣeka rite, meditation and worship are said to consist of twenty syllables.
The house of one who devotes himself to the mantra through recitation, fire-offerings, worship,
and meditation becomes filled with jewels, gold, and grain, without end.

The earth, abounding with all kinds of crops, shall belong to him; endowed with sons and friends, he attains the supreme goal at the end. Having worshipped Govinda in the fire with white flowers and rice grains, [he attains that same state].
Having offered ten thousand oblations with clarified butter, one should apply the ashes to one's head;
for such a person, there shall be abundance of food and other provisions, and all women will be under his control.
Alternatively, one should offer a hundred thousand oblations with clarified butter, or with red lotuses soaked in the three sweets (honey, sugar, and ghee).
By means of that [offering], his sovereignty becomes as Indra's, and his prosperity certainly makes even a blade of grass seem like a mountain.
To obtain white garments and the like, one should offer oblations with white flowers and the like,
smeared with the three sweets (*trimadhu*) or anointed with clarified butter (*ājya*), numbering one thousand or eight hundred.

He who daily offers one thousand and eight oblations of white flowers sprinkled with honey in brief shall become the domestic priest of a king. [The details regarding] recitation, meditation, and the fire-oblation, as prescribed for the eighteen classes of mantras, are as follows: [Note: The text provided consists of two lines. The first line describes the ritual of offering flowers to attain the position of a royal priest. The second line refers to the general procedure for recitation, meditation, and homa according to the eighteen-fold classification of mantras.]
One should perform the ritual action with this [mantra]; it is also proclaimed here for those two [deities].
"Obeisance to Śrī-Śaktismara-Kṛṣṇa-Govinda" is the head-mantra (śiromanu).
It consists of twelve syllables, its meter is the Brāhmī Gāyatrī, and its seer and other [constituent elements] are Kṛṣṇa and so forth.
The six limbs (aṅgas) are proclaimed by means of the seed-syllables consisting of three Vedas and two pairs of phonemes.
The rites of recitation, meditation, fire-offering, and worship are declared to consist of twenty syllables.
Let this mantra be practiced by wise men who desire all forms of sovereign power.

The ten-syllable mantra begins with *Śrī*, *Śakti*, *Kāma*, and *Pūrva* (A), followed by *Uṅga* (Ū), *Janma* (E), *Śakti* (AI), and ending with *Amā* (Ā). If this same mantra is joined at the beginning with *Śakti* (AI) and *Amā* (Ā), these two mantras become the modified forms (*vikṛti*) consisting of nine syllables; they are the presiding deities of the *Cakra* and so forth, along with their limbs (*aṅgin*).
Then, during the sacrificial rite described in the twenty verses, one should meditate upon Acyuta as he embraces his beloved,
who is pressed against his own body; she holds a lotus and a blue lily in her hands, while he, radiant with the best of discs, embraces her with his two hands granting boons and fearlessness.
One should recite [the mantra] one million times and perform a thousand-fold oblation with clarified butter;
these two mantras are perfected for men in matters such as all prosperity and good fortune.
[The first is] preceded by Māra-śakti-rāmā, and [the second is] preceded by Śakti-śrī-māra.
The three ten-syllable mantras are preceded by Śrī-Śaktimāra;
for these excellent mantras, the ritual limbs (aṅgas), seers (ṛṣis), and so forth are as in the case of the ten-syllable mantra.
[He is] reddish-brown, bearing a conch, a discus, a bow, an arrow, a noose, and a goad.
Kṛṣṇa, holding a flute with both arms, should be meditated upon in the first [mantra] as being like the sun;
in the second, he is like a twenty-syllable mantra;
and in the third, he is like a ten-syllable mantra, with worship accompanied by the ornaments, the guardians of the directions, and so forth.
One should recite [the mantra] five hundred thousand times and then offer ten thousand oblations of milk-rice (pāyasa);
thereafter, the mantras become perfected for men, granting their desires along with their fulfillment. The eighteen-syllable mantra ending in the syllable *māra* bestows sons and wealth.
The limbs (*aṅga*) of this mantra, consisting of eighteen syllables beginning with *ṛṣi*, are assigned in sequence by means of the vowels mounted upon the *māra* [consonants].
Its worship is performed together with the limbs, the guardians of the directions (*dikpāla*), and so forth.
Joyfully bearing in his right hand a mass of milk-rice infused with flavor, and in his left holding fresh butter resembling the orb of the autumn moon;
wearing on his neck a lotus-stalk bracelet of brilliant luster, the god is clothed in divine garments.
May the child of Yaśodā grant us happiness.
Having worshipped Govinda daily for thirty-two lakhs [of recitations],
one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with ten parts of white sugar, clarified butter, and milk-rice.
Having worshipped the God seated upon a lotus, one should offer libations (tarpaṇa) into His lotus-face.

One desiring a son should propitiate the God with milk, plantain-paste, curd, and fresh butter; from such fasting, one obtains a son. Whatever one desires, all that is accomplished simply through this propitiation.
The Vāgbhava [seed-syllable], the Kāma-bīja, "Kṛṣṇāya," Bhuvaneśvarī,
"Govindāya," Ramā, "Gopījana-vallabhāya," and Śiva accompanied by the fourteenth vowel (au), followed by Śukra and the Sarga (ḥ).
The twenty-two-syllable mantra bestows the state of Lord of Speech (Vāgīśatva).
Like that which consists of eighteen syllables, its limbs, seers, and so forth are the same.
Worship is said to be as described for the twenty-syllable mantra; now the ritual application (pratipatti) is being told.
In her upper left hand she holds the book containing the entire essence of knowledge (*vidyā*),
and in her upper right hand a crystal rosary consisting of the *mātṛkās*.
Her two lower hands are marked with a flute composed of the *śabdabrahman*.

One should always worship Hari, who is singing, dressed in yellow garments, dark-complexioned with a tender luster, adorned with a crest of peacock feathers, the omniscient one, and served by hosts of sages who know all the Vedas.
Having thus meditated upon Bhuvaneśvara, who is possessed of the playful grace of a young woman,
the practitioner, well-restrained, should recite this mantra four hundred thousand times;
and with palāśa flowers dipped in honey, he should offer forty thousand oblations.

One should offer oblations with this rite; Manu will certainly become perfected. For that practitioner whose intellect is proficient in this, who dwells within the cavern of the crooked [path], his speech, consisting of prose and verse, flows like the current of the Gaṅgā.
May he who is learned in all the Vedas, the Shastras, and the musical arts,

having attained supreme prosperity, reach the highest state at the end; [the mantra being] *tāraṃ* (om), *hṛt* (namaḥ), *bhagavān* (bhagavate), *ṅenta* (vāsudevāya), and likewise the words *nandaputra*.
At the end of *nanda* is *vapuṣe*; at the end of *asthi-agni-māyā* are ten syllables.
This [mantra] consists of twenty-eight syllables; one should then utter the thirty-two-syllable [mantra]:
the word *nandaputra* ending in the *ṅ* case-ending (*nandaputrāya*), and likewise the word *śyāmalāṅga*.
Likewise, Bālavapuḥ, Kṛṣṇa, and Govinda consist of ten syllables.
For these two, the seer is the sage Nārada; the meters are Uṣṇih and Anuṣṭubh.
Worship is performed with the limbs beginning with Ācakra and with the guardians of the directions (dikpālas) and so forth.
One should meditate upon Hari, holding a jeweled goblet in his right hand and a golden staff in his left, embraced by the two goddesses;
one should mutter the two excellent mantras a hundred thousand times and offer ten thousand oblations of milk-rice.

Thus, the practitioner who has mastered this mantra shall become a possessor of sovereignty over the three worlds. [The mantra is: Tāra (Oṃ), enriched with the seed-syllable of Śrī-Śakti (Hrīṃ), followed by the word "namo bhagavate," then the word "nandaputra" ending in the letter Ṅ (Nandaputrāya), and joined with the face and orb of the Earth-bearer (Bhūdhārā) [namely, the syllables Ra and Ma].
At the end of the word *māṃsa*, the mantra of the body consists of nineteen syllables;
its seer is Brahmā, its metre is Anuṣṭubh, and the rest has been declared as before.
This mantra should be practiced for the sake of attaining all prosperity and accomplishments.

The syllable *tāram* (oṃ), followed by the heart-mantra (*hṛdbhava*) ending in *ṅe*, and likewise *rukmiṇīvallabhaḥ* with *śivaḥ* (namaḥ) at the end— this sixteen-syllable mantra known as *Rukmiṇīvallabha* bestows all prosperity; Nārada is remembered as its sage (*muni*).
The meter is Anuṣṭubh, the presiding deity is Hari, the beloved of Rukmiṇī;
its five limbs consist of one, four, one, four, and two syllables respectively.

Embracing with his left arm his beloved, whose complexion is like the *tāpiñja* flower, who possesses a golden luster, and whose left hand displays a blossoming lotus, [he sits] upon the *sacintāmaṇi* stone.
May Hari protect you for a long time— He who embraces her while holding a golden staff in His other hand, wearing yellow garments of the *aśoka* flower and various ornaments.
Having thus meditated upon the Lord of Rukmiṇī, one should recite this mantra one hundred thousand times.
A person should offer ten thousand oblations with red lotuses soaked in honey;
he should daily worship Him with His limbs [the deities of the mantra] and with Nārada and the other guardians of the directions,
as well as with the Vajra and other [weapons], for the attainment of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
"Holding a playful staff, with His arm embraced by the women of the cowherds,
He who has the form of a child at the end of the staff, O dark as a cloud"—
this is the mantra ending with the word "Bhagavan Viṣṇu" and concluding with the wife of Fire (Svāhā).
This mantra consists of twenty-nine syllables; its sage is said to be Nārada, its meter is Anuṣṭubh, and its deity is Hari bearing the playful staff (Līlādaṇḍadhara).
The performance of the limb-assignments (aṅgakriyā) is considered to be by means of syllables numbering four, four, eleven, four, and four respectively.
May the Lord of wide strides, who has slain Kaṃsa, protect you— he who bewilders the young cowherd girls with the playful staff of his own hand,
and the beautiful women of the city with his left hand, while pointing with his right hand toward his dear friend, the goddess Śrī.

Having meditated thus, one should mutter [the mantra] one hundred thousand times or ten thousand times with sesame seeds and rice grains smeared with the three sweets; one should offer oblations and perform worship of the limbs [of the deity] along with the guardians of the quarters and others.
Whoever indeed constantly worships Hari with devotion during the *līlā-daṇḍa* is honored by all the worlds; Indirā always worships him.
He is endowed with the thirteen vowels, possesses the Śārṅga bow, and is accompanied by Medas and Keśava.
Likewise, the mantra consists of seven syllables: *māṃsa-yugaṃ bhā-ya-śiraḥ*.

Its limbs (*aṅga*) are formed with the [mantras] beginning with *ā-cakra*. Nārada is remembered as its sage (*ṛṣi*); the meter (*chandas*) is *uṣṇih*, and Govallabha is declared to be its deity (*devatā*).
The one to be meditated upon is Acyuta, seated in the midst of a herd of tawny cows, calling out to her while holding a flute in his right hand;
in his other hand he holds a noose with a staff, possessing the grace of a rain-cloud, clad in yellow garments, and adorned with a crest made of the feathers of the enemy of serpents (the peacock).
One should recite this mantra one hundred thousand times and perform seven thousand oblations.
Having worshipped the eight groups of cows in the midst of the limbs and the guardians of the directions using cow’s milk,
he who offers oblations with milk one thousand and eight times every day—
From that [six-syllable mantra], one becomes rich with herds of cattle; this is the ritual procedure for the ten-syllable mantra.

With the *salava* (the seed-syllable) and *vāsudeva* extracted, followed by the word *bhagavat* ending in the dative case (*-e*), and likewise the word *śrīgovinda*, this twelve-syllable mantra is thus proclaimed.

One may perform the ritual visualization with Manu, Nārada, Gāyatrī, Kṛṣṇa as the seers (ṛṣis), and the Cakra (rathāṅga) as the meter; one may also employ the single syllable, the individual letters, or all of them together.
I bow to Him who is dark-blue in luster, seated upon a jeweled lion-throne at the foot of the Kalpa tree.
I meditate upon Murāri, who wears yellow garments and holds a conch and a lotus-staff in his lotus-like hands;

who is surrounded by cows with flowing milk; who is bathed by streams of nectar falling from the jars held in the outstretched hands of the lords of the gods; and whose eyes resemble the petals of a fresh lotus.

Having meditated thus and recited the *acyuta-mantra* one hundred thousand times, one should then perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) with milk twelve thousand times daily. One should worship this [deity] daily,
whether it is installed in a cow-pen, in one's own home, or in images and the like.
Furthermore, those attendants of Viṣṇu, together with their entire retinue, are to be worshipped;
they are to be worshipped at the door, on the threshold, and on the seats, and the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa) is to be worshipped in front of them.
Caṇḍa and Pracaṇḍa are in the east, and Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ are in the south.
Jaya and Vijaya are in the west, while Bala and Prabala are in the north.
Having worshipped Dvāraśrī above, one should worship these [deities] in pairs at the door. Vāstu-puruṣa is to be worshipped there, in the middle of the pedestal of the door.
On the two sides at the end of the door, one should worship Gaṅgā and Yamunā as prescribed;
in the corners, one should worship Vighna, Durgā, Vāṇī, and Kṣetreśa.
With a concentrated mind, one should worship Vāstupuruṣa in the center of the house.

Having uttered the *tāra* (om), the word *śārṅga* ending in the dative (*-e*), followed by the syllable *sa* with the preceding vowel and *śara*, along with the *savāsana* [mantra], and having said *hūṃ phaṭ namas*, one stands before Hari with the *astra-mudrā*.
Then, while seated in a composed posture, one should scatter flowers and unbroken rice-grains (akṣata) in all directions.

This practice is to be performed everywhere, especially when [the deities] have been installed. Having completed the self-worship up to that point, one should then [worship] the gurus' wives as previously described.
Having worshipped the venerable Guru, the primordial ancestors, all my predecessors, their sandals, Nārada and others who are the ancient Siddhas,
and thereafter the Bhāgavatas, one should worship Vighna to the south.
Having worshipped the pedestal as before, one should worship Śrī Govinda;
then Rukmiṇī and Satyabhāmā on the two sides, Indra in front, and Surabhi behind; and having worshipped the deities of the limbs in the filaments [of the lotus].
One should worship [the deities] beginning with Hṛt and ending with Varman in the cardinal directions, and Astra in the intermediate corners.

Then, the six Śaktis—Kālindī, Rohiṇī, Nāgnajitī, and the others—are to be worshipped on the petals. Furthermore, Dāmā and the others, including Kiṅkiṇī, are to be worshipped at the corners of the pedestal.

One should then worship Damodara and others, the staff and the bamboo, Śrīvatsa and Kaustubha in front, and the forest garland (vanamālā) at the forefront; thereafter, one should worship them in the eight directions:
Pāñcajanya, the mace, the discus, Vasudeva, and Devakī.
[Namaskāra] to Nanda-gopa and Yaśodā, along with the cowherds and gopīs;
to Indra and the others, as well as Kumuda and the others; and likewise to Viṣvaksena in the north.
[The gatekeepers are] Kumuda, Kumudākṣa, Puṇḍarīka, and Vāmana.
Śaṅkukarṇa, Sarvanetra, Sumukha, and Supratiṣṭhita— these [deities] reside in the cow-pen; one should worship Śrī Govinda there daily, who bestows nectar upon the gopīs, once, twice, or thrice a day.
Long-lived and free from disease, endowed with cattle, grain, wealth, and the like,
and enriched by sons, friends, and kinsmen, he finally attains the supreme state.
He who possesses upper teeth, the Śārṅga bow, the discus, and a mark on the right ear [attains this].
The eight-syllable root mantra, ending with *namo māṃsanāthāya*,
has Brahmā as its seer (*ṛṣi*), the Gāyatrī as its meter (*chandaḥ*), and Kṛṣṇa as its deity (*devatā*).
The five limbs (*aṅga*) are said to be formed by pairs of syllables from the entire mantra.
Meditating upon the cowherd boy— five years of age, exceedingly proud, running about in the courtyard with eyes clouded by dust,
and adorned with tinkling bells, bracelets, necklaces, and anklets—
one should mutter the mantra eight hundred thousand times, or at least one thousand times.
One should offer oblations with fuel-sticks from the *brahmavṛkṣa* tree or with milk-rice (*pāyasa*).

One should worship Kṛṣṇa, who has been installed in the temple, daily with this [rite]. Having performed the worship of the door and so forth, ending with the worship of the pedestal (*pīṭha*), according to the prescribed method.
One should worship Hari in the center, and the limbs (aṅgas) in due order in the cardinal and intermediate directions:
Vāsudeva, Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha;
as well as Rukmiṇī, Satyabhāmā, Lakṣmaṇā, and Jāmbavatī.
One should worship these deities, beginning with Indravajra, in the cardinal and intermediate directions outside.
He who constantly recites this mantra while worshipping Hari according to the prescribed rite shall be endowed with all prosperity and shall eternally attain the pure state.
At the end of *tāra* (oṃ), *śrī*, *śakti* (hrīṃ), and *māra* (klīṃ), one should utter the word *śrīkṛṣṇāya*.
Above that, [one should say] *śrīgovindāya* and also *śrīgopījana*.
Then *vallabhāya*, followed by *strīḥ* and *śrīṃ*; this is the mantra of Siddhagopāla.

One should recite while remembering Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, who are seated in the Mādhavī bower, protected by Garuḍa, and fully absorbed in divine play. The mantra consisting of the syllables "sarga" (sa), "eka" (e), and "arṇa" (a)— namely *sakṣama*— joined with the eight vowels (*vasusvara*) and the discus (*cakrī*), is considered the mantra.

The two-syllabled mantra is "Kṛṣṇa"; that same one becomes three-syllabled when preceded by "Kāma" (Kāmākṛṣṇa); that same one becomes four-syllabled when ending in the dative case (Kṛṣṇāya). Another four-syllabled mantra will be mentioned: "Kṛṣṇāya namaḥ," which consists of five syllables.

The other five-syllabled mantra is "kṛṣṇāya" placed between the two seed-syllables of Smara (Klīm). The six-syllabled mantra is declared to be "gopālāya" followed by the two fire-born wives (Svāhā). Another [six-syllabled mantra] begins with the seed-syllable of Smara and ends with the fire-born wife (Svāhā).

The six-syllabled mantra was previously mentioned; furthermore, "Kṛṣṇa" and "Govinda," each with the dative case ending, constitute a seven-syllabled mantra. Another seven-syllabled mantra is stated by others as "Śrī-śakti-māra-kṛṣṇāya," where "māra" consists of seven syllables.
The first group of eight syllables consists of *kṛṣṇagovindau* ending in the dative case (*ṅe*), followed by *smarādyā*.
The second group of eight consists of *dadhibhakṣaṇam* with the dative suffix (*ṅe*) and the wife of fire (*vahnijāyā*).
The third group of eight is declared as *suprasannātmane namaḥ*.

The root mantra previously mentioned consists of nine syllables and is joined with the word *smara*. Another nine-syllable mantra consists of the words "Kṛṣṇa" and "Govinda," both ending in the dative case (*ṅe*) and followed by "namaḥ.
The ten-syllable mantra is: *klīṃ glauṃ klīṃ syāmalāṅgāya namaḥ*.
The mantra "Śiro'ntavālavapuṣe Kṛṣṇāya" is considered by Manu;
the mantra "Śiro'ntavālavapuṣe Klīṃ Kṛṣṇāya" is remembered by the wise.
This eleven-syllable mantra has Nārada as its sage (ṛṣi).
The meter is the goddess Gāyatrī, and the deity is Kṛṣṇa as impelled [by the mantra]. Then, one should meditate upon that Hari, whose limbs are formed by the six syllables with their long vowels.
May He protect [us]—He who has the luster of a blooming blue lotus, whose eyes are like red lotuses, and who stands upon the lotus-like calves and shanks of Balarāma.
May Mukunda, whose waist is adorned with tinkling bells,
who holds fresh butter and pure milk-rice in his two arms,
who is worshipped by the entire world, and whose neck is graced by ornaments and the shining nails of the cowherds and cowherdesses— may he protect you for a long time.
Having meditated thus, one should then mutter a hundred thousand times the mantra of these [deities];
thereafter, one should offer ten thousand oblations of milk-rice mixed with ghee and white sugar.
One should perform the libation for these mantras as many times as the number of oblations offered.
One who worships with great concentration should perform the daily libation (tarpaṇa) as prescribed;
one should worship the limbs beginning from the fire (Agni) and ending with Īśāna, starting from the heart-mantra (hṛdaya) and ending with the armor-mantra (kavaca);
one should worship the eye-mantra (netra) in front, and again outside in the cardinal directions.
Indra, Vajra, and the others are to be worshipped; this is declared to be their ritual service.
Thus, the best of those who know the mantras should devote himself to one of these mantras. All his goals are within the reach of his hand, and he is honored by men.
I shall now declare another four-syllabled mantra that bestows immediate fruit.
It is proclaimed with the word "Kṛṣṇa" situated between two "Umās.
Its seer and other attributes, as well as the six limbs, are stated to be as previously described.

May Vāsudeva protect you—he who is seated upon the shimmering pericarp of the lotus sprouting from the root of the glorious Kalpa-tree; who has been consecrated with jewels as numerous as the pollen-dust within the lotuses hanging from its branches; and who, golden-hued, illuminates the entire three worlds with his radiant splendors.
That self-controlled one, subsisting on milk-rice and the like, fresh butter, and nectar,
should meditate thus and recite the mantra four hundred thousand times; thereafter,
he should perform forty thousand oblations with bilva fruits smeared with the three sweets (trimadhu).

Having offered libations daily with water— consecrated by the limbs [of the mantra], the treasures, Indra and the other deities, and the thunderbolt and other weapons— as recited in the words [of the mantra], one should satisfy Kṛṣṇa with the thought that it possesses the three sweet flavors (milk,
sugar, and ghee). If one desires to kill him, there is another mantra beginning with "māra" for the consumption of his flesh and blood.
The six limbs of this crest-jewel of mantras are dark;

he is mounted upon a golden swing shimmering at the top of a wish-fulfilling tree in a slightly reddish garden, being gazed upon by two gopīs, and possessing the luster of a blooming fresh bandhūka flower and vermilion.
I pay homage to her whose hair is lovely with playful curls, and who is adorned with a multitude of small bells shimmering upon the slope of her waist.
Having thus meditated upon Mukunda, who is radiant with the Śārdūla, Kāmāṅkuśa, Lasita, Gadā, and Kalpa [mudrās],
and having recited this previously prepared [mantra], one should offer oblations with fresh blue lotuses mixed with the three sweets; then, as before, one should gratify Hari.
One should daily offer one hundred and eight oblations of red rice-ears mixed with the three sweets, using each of the two mantras.
By means of this mandala, the earth— along with its noble and ignoble rulers— [is subdued].
That house shall quickly become filled with heaps of rice for one who practices devotion to either of these two mantras through recitation, worship, oblations, and so forth. Such a person,
devoted to the Self, shall become as eloquent among women as the god of love is glorious, and even in the face of physical calamity, he shall remain so.
[This concludes] that which is called Mahācyuta. Thus ends the seventh chapter in the Kramadīpikā.
Now, the procedure for subjugation (vaśya) is described, [derived] from the previously mentioned ten-syllable mantra and the eighteen-syllable mantra.

Having worshipped Mukunda at the beginning of the day with pure wild flowers in full bloom— He who, by His mere remembrance, always ordains the state of being beloved by the entire world for every human being— and having performed the daily rites with delight, one should then fulfill the duties prescribed for midday.

One who recites this mantra, which possesses eight qualities and consists of ten syllables, shall certainly bring about subjugation; such a practitioner will surely make even the most eloquent of men subject to his will through various mandalas.
With *jāti* flowers, one should visualize the excellent cowherd boy engaged in play with the flowers of the enemy of the red-horsed one (the blue lotus).
Having performed the rite with blue lotuses as described before, one shall bring kings and others under control in due order;
furthermore, by daily offering a thousand oblations for seven nights consisting of white flowers combined with rice grains sprinkled with clarified butter, [the same result is achieved].
He who wears that ash on his hairline and forehead subdues even a young woman; she likewise subdues men in the same way.
Betel, clothing, flowers, collyrium, sandalwood, and so forth, when consecrated more than a thousand times with either of the two mantras, [achieve the same].
To whomever he gives it, that wise man shall quickly become a servant to him; indeed, there is no need for deliberation in this matter.
Whether at the king’s gate, in legal proceedings, in an assembly, at a gambling match, or in debate, whoever possesses [this] one hundred and eight [verses]—
Having recited [the mantra], one should indeed utter the first word; he shall then abide there and there above.

Having remembered the Slayer of Mura seated at the foot of a Kadamba tree, singing most sweetly with the women of Vraja, and having offered oblations into the fire with peacock feathers mixed with honey, the knower of mantras brings the three worlds under his control.
He who, remembering Acyuta situated in the midst of the *rāsa* dance, should daily recite the ten-syllable mantra one thousand times for ten months, shall obtain his desired maiden. She, too,
who meditates day by day upon Acyuta seated atop a lofty bower, [reciting] a thousand times...
She recites it eight times, for by that the maiden obtains her desired boon from the mandala.

Having meditated upon Him, the Lord of the beautiful women of Vraja, as He dances while holding the hands of those women, the knower of mantras should recite this excellent mantra of eighteen syllables one hundred thousand times.

Alternatively, having offered ten thousand oblations of parched grain or *karṇaka* flowers mixed with honey, one should recite the mantra for that long until the desired maiden is soon brought as a bride;
likewise, one may perform libations with eighteen-syllable mantras using *bilva* wood fuel smeared with the three sweets (*trimadhu*).

To bring the twice-born under one's control, one should offer ten thousand oblations with *kuśa* grass, sesame seeds, or rice grains. One should subjugate kings with oblations made of *kṛtamāla*, *kuruṇṭaka*, and *vakula* flowers; likewise, one may subjugate commoners (*viś*) with oblations of *akṣa* and *pāṭala* flowers, and others in the same manner.
With fresh red lotuses and blue water-lilies, as well as sweet-scented campaka and pāṭala flowers, one should summon ten thousand celestial nymphs,
such as the daughter of Brahmā (Sarasvatī) and others, in due order to bring them under control within a short time.
With fresh flowers of the *hayāri* (karavīra), soaked in the three sweets (honey, sugar, and ghee), one should daily summon a thousand [beings] for the duration of a day of the sages (seven days).
At midnight,
Mercury, with a mind full of pride, forcibly and suddenly makes a courtesan— who is tormented by the arrows of Love— his own servant.

For one who performs oblations at night three hundred and ten times with white mustard seeds mixed with pungent substances and made very moist with the three sweets (*trimadhu*), even Indra, the beloved of Śacī, becomes subject to his will; how much more so others?
Furthermore, by performing oblations with bilva fruits, fuel-sticks, flowers, and leaves, all rapidly melted with honey—
With lotuses accompanied by white unbroken rice grains, one shall quickly bring Kamalā under control for a long time.

Having stolen the garments of cowherd women and mounted a kadamba tree, one should recite the mantra a thousand times at night while remembering Acyuta with a focused heart; thus, even Urvaśī will be forcibly brought under one's power within ten days.

What is the use of speaking further here? Of these two mantras, there is indeed no other superior for subjugating even those women who are skilled in the art of seduction and whose armor consists of the weapons of the flower-armed god [Kāma].
I bow to the youthful one, white as the *kunda* flower and the moon, whose eyes have the luster of the petals of a red lotus, and who holds the discus and the conch.
I bow to Mukunda, who holds a lotus and a mace with his long, staff-like arms;
who is radiant with divine ornaments, unguents, and a garland shimmering like a fresh stalk;
who is resplendent in his shining yellow garments; and who sits upon a lotus, surrounded by sages.
Having meditated thus upon the Primordial Being seated upon the lotus-throne of his own radiant heart—
possessing the luster of a dense lotus or resembling molten gold— one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times.
Then, interspersed with two *tārās* (the syllables *oṃ* and *svāhā*), one should offer oblations into the fire one thousand times using fuel-sticks of milky trees.
Then, with offerings of milk-rice mixed with honey, ghee, and sugar— or even with plain milk-rice—
one should meditate upon the Lord of the World, whose form is eternal bliss, who dwells within the lotus of one's own heart,
and who is the sun that dispels all duality.
Meditating upon Him with one-pointed concentration, the pure-minded person should daily recite the mantra three thousand times and perform worship according to the ritual prescribed for the evening.
He who, with a steady mind, constantly devotes himself to this rite with devotion, [crosses] the terrifying ocean of worldly existence.

Having crossed over the vast expanse of the ocean, which is spread wide with the swarms of crocodiles that are sense-objects and with towering waves known as birth and death, he attains the supreme abode of bliss belonging to Hari.
He who constantly chants His names, listens to His stories, remembers His forms,
and bows at His lotus feet with humility born of devotion— he alone is worthy of worship by the wise; he alone is eternally liberated.
I shall now briefly declare another pair of mantras, which is a supreme secret named *Bhuvanamohana*.

The first consists of fourteen syllables (the number of Brahmā, Indra, Vāmana, and the moon), while the other is preceded by that [first] and consists of twenty-one syllables (the number of the sky, the sense-organs, and the Lord of Śaṅkha).
Regarding these two mantras, the sage is said by the wise to be Sammohana Nārada, and the meter is declared to be Gāyatrī.
Now, Viṣṇu, the Enchanter of the Three Worlds, shall be the deity for these two; next, the six-limbed [mantra] is described.

With the long vowels beginning with the non-neuter [consonants], accompanied by the *lavas* (nasals) and mounted upon the *kalās*, one should perform the ritual as previously stated, up to the placement of the seat (*āsana*). Then, however:
Having placed the six limbs upon the palms and the fingers of both hands as arrows,

one should assign the limbs to the parts of the body using the letters of the Mātṛkā interspersed with the mantra. One should then place those arrows, ending in *namaḥ* and suffixed with the dative case (*ṅe*), upon the head, heart, eyes, and feet by means of the fingers of the hands.
Drying, enchanting, inflaming, heating, and intoxicating—
these five are proclaimed in sequence as the primary rites, beginning with the syllables *drāṃ*, *drīṃ*, *klīṃ*, *vlūṃ*, and *saḥ*.
Then, with a concentrated mind, one should meditate upon Puruṣottama, the deluder of the worlds,
seated upon a jeweled lotus-throne shining on a ground made of gems, beneath a magnificent great Kalpa-tree in a most divine celestial grove.

The son of Aṅga beheld the Lord seated upon a lofty throne made of excellent parijāta wood; He is the life-breath of the universe, possessing the immediate radiance of a rising sun, and is of golden hue.
He holds in His hands the discus, sword, goad, noose, beautiful flowers, arrows, sugarcane-bow, lotus, and mace.
Holding with His own arms a pair of lotus-eyes that are reddish, long, wide, and rolling;
blazing with a jeweled crown, earrings, necklaces, armlets, bracelets, wave-patterned waistbands, girdles, and other ornaments;
and clothed in yellow garments, He is further illuminated by reddish garlands and unguents.
[He saw] Kamalā, seated upon his own left thigh, embracing him while holding a lotus in her left hand;
her womb was moist with passion, and the creeper-like body of the goddess was radiant, agitated by the intoxication of love.

[He saw] a young woman, adorned with beautiful ornaments, garlands, and unguents, draped in pure white garments; her restless, white-lotus-like eyes were like bees hovering over the lotus of his own face,
as he firmly embraced her with his left arm, which held a stalk of sugarcane.

His heart overflowing with supreme bliss born thereof, he was surrounded by thousands of women from among the gods, *diti*-born demons, serpents, *guhyakas*, and *gandharvas*— the sole teachers of all that moves and is stationary—
whose limbs were languid with intoxication and passion, and who shone with divine ornaments.

Having meditated upon the single syllable or the eight-syllable mantra as non-different from one's own self, one should mutter it for one million days. One should perform oblations with *kiṃśuka* blossoms sprinkled with the three sweets,
a thousand times the number of suns (one million), and likewise satisfy [the deity] with pure waters that many times.
In the yantra proclaimed with twenty syllables, one should worship this [deity] daily with devotion until the end of the fortnight;
by this, Śiva becomes propitiated for the king. Having mounted Hari upon his shoulder, one should worship him with offerings beginning with *arghya* and ending with incense.
He placed his limbs and arrows according to the sequence of ritual placement (*nyāsa*); he placed the crown upon his head,
earrings upon his ears, weapons in his hands,
the *śrīvatsa* and *kaustubha* gems upon his chest, and the forest garland upon his upper body and in the water.
Having worshipped the one clad in yellow garments on the left hip with his own seed-syllable, as well as Śrī,
one should then worship the limbs (aṅgas) in the intermediate directions and the cardinal directions within the pericarp, the arrows (iṣus) in the cardinal directions,
the fifth [limb] in the corners, and furthermore, the powers (śaktis) in the petals starting from the southeast.
Lakṣmī and Sarasvatī are golden-hued; Rati and Prīti are deep red;
Kīrti and Śānti are white; and Tuṣṭi and Puṣṭi are like emeralds.
Their limbs are adorned with divine unguents, emerald ornaments, garlands, and silk garments, and their tresses are beautifully decorated.

With smiling faces, afflicted by love, and holding beautiful chowries in their lovely hands—these are the Lokeshas to be worshipped outside; thus has the worship extracted from the two mantras been described.
Generally, the ritual for Purushottama is not stated here in such detail because it has already been extensively explained.
Having uttered "To the Enchanter of the Three Worlds," then "We know" for Smara, then "We meditate upon," and thereafter "May Viṣṇu impel that for us"—
this [gāyatrī] is to be chanted at the beginning of recitation; it removes misfortune and bestows fortune through chanting, worship, and fire-offerings.

One should sprinkle the materials for the self-sacrifice (ātma-yāga) and the ritual substances for the worship with water for the sake of purification. He who daily at dawn satisfies the two mantras with a hundred [offerings] and with ten thousand flowers using water, effortlessly obtains his desired objects.

Having offered ten thousand oblations into the fire with clarified butter accompanied by the *sampāta* residue, and having likewise consecrated [the food] with the same mantra, let him feed [the woman] while she is in a state of equanimity; for even a lover of beautiful women can thus be brought under one's control. Furthermore, the rites prescribed in the eighteen-syllable mantra should be performed by these two to achieve subjugation (*vaśya*).
In this world, there is no other equal to these two mantras for the rite of subjugating the three worlds.

Here, one should meditate upon Kṛṣṇa accompanied by the song of his flute during the recitation of the single-syllable mantra; or else, one may meditate on Kandarpa (the God of Love), whose limbs and attire possess a reddish luster, and who holds a noose, a goad, and a bow.
The practitioner of mantra who, possessing a pure intellect, constantly recites one of these two *manus*,
attains exceedingly vast accomplishment even in the hereafter.
Now, *satya* and *śauri* are the third and fourth.
Adorned with the crest of fire, the dwarf, the eye, and the crescent moon;
victory to you, O Kṛṣṇa, whose forms consist of the pairs, the uninterrupted self-born, fire, power, mouth, circle, power, and letters!
Within the *praṇava*, for the one whose mind is joyful, there follow the syllables of the wind, the moon, the teacher, and the vital breath.
That [mantra] consists of the fourth [vowel], the black syllable, the bow, the ten colors, and the best of men;
it is encapsulated by the syllables of the daughter of the mountain (L), the ocean (M), and Rāma (R), arranged in both direct and reverse order.
Thus extracted, this mantra of forty-eight syllables is a treasury of poetry, a source of delight for Lakṣmī, and a destroyer of sins.
The sage Nārada, possessing a face of sixty-four syllables, is said here to be the meter;

its presiding deity is indeed Hari, known as the "Deluder of the Three Worlds," as proclaimed by the sages. The *tripuṭa* (three-part) arrangement consists of the syllables of the *mantra*—eight, five, seven, eight, and ten—each situated separately.

It is taught that the six-limbed [rite] is endowed with one's own caste; indeed, that is the pleasing of people through ritual action alone. Then, having thoroughly purified the body according to the path of liberation, and having consecrated the seat (pīṭha) by means of one's own armor-mantra, one should place the five arrows of the bodiless god (Anaṅga) along with the six limbs upon the two hands according to the sequence of the ten-syllable rite.
With this [mantra], let him fill the entire body on all sides with the *smarasaṃpuṭa* [mantras] and subsequently with the letters of the *mātṛkā*.
Then, he should perform that which is proclaimed as the ten syllables beginning with the ten *tattvas*, ending with the *mūrttipañjara*.
Having performed the creation, sustenance, the ten [syllables], the six limbs, and the arrows, he should then perform everything else as previously described.

Having made a vow and remembering Mukunda— the sole witness of all worlds— those of faultless and steady intellect [reside] in a city adorned with mountain caves, possessing lofty sal-tree gate-towers and broad streets,
crowded with white palaces kissed by clouds, and featuring expansive jeweled mansions with wide door-sills.
It was resplendent with thousands of diverse dwellings belonging to the twice-born, kings, merchants, and those born of the Śūdra caste, as well as the houses of artisans;
it was further adorned by thousands of shining abodes for goats, frequented by elephants, horses, camels, donkeys, and cows;
and it was filled with the accumulation of wealth resulting from the buying and selling conducted by great merchants gathered in various marketplaces.
In his own city, which was adorned with beautiful mansions of lovely women skilled in captivating the minds of men,
with wide and clear paths where the nectar of blooming lotuses— red as vermilion— was being greedily sought,
and where the quarters were made resonant by birds bearing the names of the kalahamsa, sārasa, and rathāṅga;

In a jeweled pavilion, filled with celestial trees whose branches were stirred by bees greedy for fragrant blossoms and which provided various objects of desire for men; where auspicious, gentle breezes caused the tips of the trees to sway; which was as bright as a thousand suns;
its interior illuminated by the light of jewel-lamps; and adorned with a wide canopy of variegated cloth spread above.
In that place, where the ground was sprinkled with highly fragrant water, adorned with festoons of various blooming flowers,
and attended by hundreds of women whose eyes rolled with intoxication, who were languid with passion, and who moved their fly-whisks with trembling hands—
[he was served] by those stumbling...
With their sweet voices and slender waists made graceful by the weight of their breasts,
they rained down an unceasing flow of jewel-like conduct; though they were pouring forth the nectar-essence of the great river of their own exhaustion, they remained below.
One should meditate upon Acyuta seated upon a broad lion-throne whose lotus-feet shine upon a jeweled ground beneath a celestial tree; he possesses the delicate complexion of a fresh blue lotus,
wears a crown adorned with curling locks of hair, and has earrings set with smiling jewels and flowers.

With a beautiful forehead and shimmering, upturned eyebrows; with large, reddish, long, and tremulous eyes; with cheeks radiant with the brilliance of jeweled earrings; with lips as red as the fresh bandhujīvaka flower;
illuminating the quarters of the sky with the moonlight of his smile; and with a face adorned by glistening drops of perspiration from the exertion of his dance.
Her garments were adorned with excellent garlands and ornaments radiant with clusters of gems whose rays were shimmering;
her body was smeared with camphor and saffron, and she shone with broad, long, and auspicious sacrificial threads.
Her lotus-feet were like young, reddish lotuses, and her two lotus-hands rested upon her lap, their limbs pressed against her own.
He embraced her, who possessed the luster of molten gold, as she sat between the thighs of Bhīṣmaka’s daughter resting upon his own lap;
he held her close as she clung to him, her broad hips moist with perspiration, while his own long, graceful arms were wrapped around her.

With her two hands [supporting her], she was overcome by an overflow of bliss; her lotus-eyes were closed, her limbs were slack, and her body was adorned with pearls in the form of drops of perspiration mixed with dense horripilation.
Having withdrawn the entire collection of external and internal senses into himself, he immerses his limbs— now free from all agitation—
in the ocean of the mass of incomparable great bliss known as Nīla;
[there he is attended] by Satyabhāmā and Jāmbavatī, who are adorned with divine silken garments and unguents.
[He was] embraced by those two [consorts] who were struck by the arrows of Love, whose lotus-faces had bees in the form of their restless eyes,
whose pairs of arms were entwined around him, whose limbs were beautiful, tender, dark, and ruddy,
and who stood at his right and left with hands radiant with lotuses.
