His lotus-face shone with the power of his two arms;

in all directions outside, the sages and ascetics heard him being praised by the lords of the sky-dwellers, whose bodies were bowed low with the weight of devotion and whose mouths were vocal with hymns of praise.
Having thus meditated upon Him— the progenitor of the three worlds— who bestows the four aims of human life pertaining to the objects of mind and speech when served continuously,
and who is immersed in the great ocean of intense bliss, established in His own stainless abode;
Having obtained initiation from his preceptor,

that man of pure intellect, having received this mantra from the Supreme Person, should recite it a hundred thousand times with devotion; even while engaged in hearing or seeing women, the practitioner of the mantra should remain mindful of his teachers.
And one should offer oblations into the fire ten times the [number of] recitations, using milk-rice mixed with sugar, honey, and ghee.

One should daily worship this [deity] upon the excellent seat first described, for the sake of liberation from impermanence. Then, beginning with the *vibhūti* [mantra], one should worship according to the sequence of ritual placement (*nyāsa*) up to the end of the arrows (*śara*).
In this excellent yantra described with twenty syllables, one should first write the Self (the central deity) along with the [deities of] the forms and so forth;
then, having written the central seed-syllable surrounded by the four seed-syllables in the directions of Varuṇa, Indu, Yama, and Indra,
one should further surround them with forty-two syllables.

One should inscribe the Vāk, Māyā, and Śrī-mantras respectively in the directions of Śiva (East), Hari (South), and Agni (Southeast); likewise, in the directions of Rakṣas (Southwest), Ambu (Northwest), and Anila (West). Having performed the remaining rites as previously described, one should duly worship the pedestal.
Having mentally conceived the form here, or having externally worshipped Him in the central seed-syllable,

one should worship the Śaktis— Rukmiṇī and the others— in sequence upon the seed-syllables of the mouth, the right, the left, and the back; then the six limbs in the six corners, and the arrows on the filaments.

In the middle of the [eight] directions beginning with Lakṣmī, one should place those [deities] starting with Agni; outside of them, the banners (ketus) headed by Dhvaja; at the front, the dark Ketu; at the back, the enemy of the moon (the Sun), ruddy and of pure red luster;
on both sides, the two Lords of Treasures (Nidhīśas), who have showered down masses of wealth in continuous streams.
One should worship Heramba, Śāstṛ, Durgā, and Viśvakṛt in the intermediate directions starting from the southeast,
and outside [the circle], Indra, Vajra, and the others, possessing the luster of coral, emerald, dūrvā grass, and gold;
this is declared to be the ritual procedure for Mukunda, accompanied by the sevenfold enclosure (āvṛti).

He who, having conquered his self, worships Acyuta with devotion and recites this supreme mantra, is honored by divine beings; he is the fierce sun for the lotuses that are the hearts and eyes of people. At the beginning of each day, one should satisfy him daily with milk mixed with white sugar as an offering.
With waters, he makes even a single drop of water possess the beauty of a hundred mouths;
with blossoms from which bees are emerging, and with flowers submerged in thick liquid sandalwood paste,
this Manu, beloved by the three worlds, becomes a king of poets who knows the number [of syllables] joined with the sacrificial oblation.

By his mere meditation, the deer-eyed women of the Thirty-three gods inevitably come under his control immediately; what then is not easily attained by a man through mantras such as those of Kāma, Ārtta, and Japa?
Strangely, even these two [the goddesses] constantly serve him, having cast aside their great natural rivalry.
May the Lord of Speech, together with Sarasvatī, the abode of lotuses, and the Chief Minister,
long protect this [king] who is utterly freed from mental anguish, physical disease, old age, untimely death, all evils, elemental spirits, poisons, misfortune, poverty, and the like.
May he live for many years, honored by virtuous sons, by his own children, and by throngs of friends, always nourished by abundant wealth,
and celebrated for his fame; for among all men, the Vaiṣṇava mantras are indeed powerful and rich with most exalted fruits.
The Gopāla mantras: among these,
this mantra known as Sammohana is most powerful here, a wish-fulfilling tree for the conception of incomparable prosperity.
That chief of mantra-practitioners who, possessing meditative concentration, worships this heart-pleasing [deity] with devotion, prostrations, recitation, oblations, sacrifices, and other rites—
his knots of all karma severed and his consciousness awakened— he indeed goes to that eternally pure state.
Having accepted one of these mantras from Murāri, and then having purified his inner self through the joyful recitation of the mantras, along with their offerings, oblations, and worship,
he becomes one whose inner soul is thoroughly cleansed and serene.

The yogi, whose conduct has not yet arisen and who withdraws from the waking state as from a dream, should first sit facing east upon his own very soft and comfortable seat; seated there with eyes gently closed, he should contemplate the entire universe—
composed of the elements, senses, and internal organs— as consisting of the forms of fire, moon, and sun at the end of the phonemes.
Having led [the soul] by means of the *dhruva* into the *pradhāna*, which consists of calculation, has the form of the seed, and is eternal;

having led it from there into the *puruṣa*, whose nature is the *bindu*; and having led that also into the *varā* (the *kalā*); then, in due order, let it dissolve into the *kāla-tattva*, and that into the *śakti*, and that into the *cid-ātman*, and finally let it dissolve into the absolute, peaceful, stainless, non-dual, and undifferentiated Abode.

Then, having withdrawn the sense of self-sufficiency even within the eternal Self— which is dense with unsurpassed great bliss, endowed with the ultimate end, and praised by the words of those preceded by Kṛṣṇa—
one should practice that supreme seed-syllable with the "Atha" and "Śala" syllables, like the currents of dark, deep sighs.
May he whose nature is incomparable supreme consciousness, for whom merit and demerit have been utterly exhausted,
become manifest. May Kāma, who wanders within the triangle of the Mūlādhāra—
resplendent with the light of the rising sun and possessing a luster like that of the young morning sun, the fire of time, the belly of the moon, and ten million rays of light— become manifest.

Having meditated upon that which is beautiful with the radiant, shimmering Bandhujīva flowers possessing the splendor of thousands of garlands of lightning, which has a Bindu pervaded by the three qualities (guṇas), and which is the sole cause for the arising and dissolution of the world;
Above that, one should contemplate the Suṣumṇā channel, which flashes brilliantly, possessing the luster of a mass of clearly radiant lightning, rising up toward the orb of the moon on the forehead;
it is pure consciousness, subtle in form, and inaccessible even to the Lord of the Three Eyes (Śiva), who has mastered all things.
May she, who is the root of all abodes, be remembered by you as she utters the syllable *hūṃ* with her face turned upward;
having led him down into the heart of a thousand-spoked red lotus shining with the orb of the full moon, she causes a stream of nectar to flow from her mouth.

Having drunk the red [light] consisting of mantra, which takes the form of a flowing stream of nectar, he should again enter his own abode; having thus caused himself to be satisfied once more, he should enter.
He who practices daily and every day thus within himself the Lord of the Seed, becomes free from old age, death, and disease.
Having conquered [the world], he— like the God of Love incarnate— shall live for a long time with his mass of hair unbound;
for from his lotus-face there issues forth speech, a most wondrous soul, with its rows of syllables and words clearly sweet.
Furthermore, all mantras are accomplished for him; he abides as the sole locus of profound bliss that crushes and brings cessation to worldly existence.
Wandering from the root-cakra, he assumes a form that is bodiless, saturated with his own radiance—the nectar of red blood.
Having meditated upon [the deity] filling the entire expanse of space and having caused [the object] to enter therein, the goals to be accomplished (sādhya) for a Vaiśya—
whether women or men, a city or even an assembly hall— will, when entered by one whose mind is sharpened,
undoubtedly become his servants for a long time, acting with sudden and constant obedience as their minds are subdued by him.

Then, within the heart-lotus— whose petals are the Lord [Viṣṇu], which is reddish like a *śatagopa* insect, and whose beautiful center is radiant with the orbs of the sun, moon, and fire— one should meditate upon this Vāsudeva, who is seated there, dark-complexioned, with tender limbs and a beautiful face.

Upon the two tips of the feet, on the stainless sprout-like toes, upon the earth where those who are weary rest, on the beautiful shell of the excellent tortoise, on the pair of forefeet, on the shapely shanks that gleam,
on the knees, on the thighs, on the excellent new saffron-colored garment, on the girdle-string, and on the navel— [The rays of the sun fall.]

Upon the line of hair on her noble navel, upon her broad chest adorned with a magnificent necklace, upon the Śrīvatsa and Kaustubha gem, and upon the arm-pits where your garland shines like a radiant lotus; upon your two arms, which are capable of protecting the world, resplendent with bracelets and gleaming with armlets— [Please provide the second half of the verse for a complete translation.]
Upon his two hands with their fingers resting [on the flute], upon the flute which resounds with a most sweet tone and enchants the entire world, upon his throat,
upon his pair of cheeks radiant and clear like those of a noble lineage,
upon his two ears, then upon his nose, upon his lotus-eyes, upon the play of his eyebrows, and upon his forehead—

May [the devotees] apply their own minds, by means of hundreds of meditations, to the various limbs of the Primordial Being in due order: to His hair, radiant with exceedingly fragrant and beautiful flowers and shimmering peacock feathers; to His reddish lower lip-sprout, upon which a flute is placed; and to the row of teeth, which is called "smile" and is like moonlight.
Until the mind dissolves into the noble, gentle smile of Hari, let one softly recite the seed-mantra of Ananga,
or else the eighteen-syllable or ten-syllable mantra, while the breath flows slowly and evenly.
Having repeatedly fixed the mind upon the lotus feet and so forth, up to the smile [of the deity],

and having dissolved it here [in that state], one whose consciousness is attenuated becomes the blissful, eternal Self. [This is the result] of the applications of recitation, fire-offerings, worship, libations, and mantra-consecrations.

This *Kramadīpikā*, which dispels the darkness of doubt, shall be illuminated by me for those who have fallen away from the *Kṛṣṇa-mantra* rites. Like a hand-held lamp, it should be held in the hands of the great ones with their own oil day and night for the attainment of all happiness.

I bow to that Lord who, though established in his own state of playful repose, fashioned the discus from the body of the enemy of Manmatha for the sake of battle— discerning it as a mere worldly convention—
and who bears a face like the radiant new moon, adorned with the syllable *Aghora* and the *Ātman*. I certainly worship him.
May that Yādava— who, having performed the crushing of his body as his own penance,
who was intent on rolling about in the lap of the cowherd girls, who has eradicated all sin, and who is the lord of the earth— bestow upon you the state of supreme joy.

I bow to that light of the nectar-like bliss of consciousness, which the Lord of the Gods approaches when afraid of the one who removes [darkness]; which the King of the sharp-rayed sun [the Sun-god] seeks among others; in whom this world moves as if pierced by a thread; which, having been produced, eternally protects what is spread out; upon which everything rests; which possesses great and blazing splendor; and which the Cowherd (Kṛṣṇa) bestows.
To Kṛṣṇa. Thus ends the eighth chapter of the Kramadīpikā.
Thus ends the *Kramadīpikā*.
Thus ends the *Kramadīpikā*, compiled and published within the collection of various Tantras such as the *Tantrasāra* and others, by the venerable Rasikamohana Caṭṭopādhyāya.
